questions.prompt: You open your eyes in the morning. What do you do first?

options.label: Open the curtains or drink some water

insight.reveal: People who start with light or water often treat the body as the first thing to care for. The same instinct tends to show up later in the day: you fix the room before you fix the problem.
insight.step: Tomorrow morning, notice the very first thought you have before you move. Just notice it.

options.label: Reach for my phone

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests your day often begins with other people's news before your own thoughts. People who do this often say their best ideas show up later, in the shower or on a walk, when the screen is gone.
insight.step: Tomorrow, wait until your feet touch the floor before you touch your phone.

options.label: Snooze, then snooze again

insight.reveal: Snoozing is a tiny daily bargain: a little comfort now, a rushed start later. People who snooze a lot often make the same trade in other places, like replying 'later' to messages they actually want to answer.
insight.step: Next time your alarm rings, sit up before you decide anything. See if the bargain feels different sitting up.

options.label: Lie still and replay yesterday or worry about today

insight.reveal: This answer tends to belong to people whose minds wake up before their bodies do. The hidden pattern: the worry usually lands on small social moments, not big problems, and it fades once your hands are busy.
insight.step: Tomorrow, when the replay starts, get up and do one physical thing, like making the bed, before you keep thinking.

questions.prompt: You miss one day of a habit you were building. What happens next?

options.label: I just pick it up again the next day

insight.reveal: People who choose this tend to judge a habit by the month, not the day. That wide view often shows up in friendships too: one missed call doesn't change how you see someone.
insight.research: In one study, new daily habits took a median of 66 days to become automatic, and missing a single day did not ruin progress.
insight.step: This week, give one habit a 'never miss twice' rule and see how it feels.

options.label: I do double the next day to make up for it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you keep a quiet ledger with yourself. People who 'pay back' missed days are often the same ones who return favours fast and feel uneasy owing anyone anything.
insight.step: Next time you miss a day, do the normal amount, not double. Notice if the ledger voice complains.

options.label: I quietly let the whole habit go

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people who see a habit as a chain: once it breaks, it's over. But the chain is mostly in the story, not the habit. The same 'all or nothing' feeling can show up in diets, studies and tidying.
insight.research: In one study, new daily habits took a median of 66 days to become automatic, and missing a single day did not ruin progress.
insight.step: Pick one habit you dropped and do the smallest version of it once this week, just one minute.

options.label: I feel it proves something about me

insight.reveal: People who choose this often turn one missed day into a verdict on their whole character. Interestingly, they tend to be very fair judges of other people's slips and very strict judges of their own.
insight.step: Next time you slip, ask: 'What would I say to a friend who missed one day?' Then say that to yourself.

questions.prompt: Your desk or table right now looks like…

options.label: Clear, with everything in its place

insight.reveal: People with a clear space often think more easily once things are put away, as if the table is part of their mind. The same people tend to tidy right before a hard task, and that's not avoidance, it's warming up.
insight.step: Before your next hard task, give yourself exactly two minutes to tidy, then start, even if it's not done.

options.label: Piles that only I understand

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you remember things by where they are, not by labels. People like this often work well with loose systems and struggle when someone 'helpfully' tidies their space.
insight.step: This week, notice how fast you can find one thing in your piles. Your system may be better than it looks.

options.label: Buried, and I'll fix it on some big day

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come with a belief in a future 'big day' when everything gets sorted. People who wait for that day often wait for it in other areas too, like inbox clean-ups or calling old friends.
insight.step: Today, clear just one corner of the table, the size of a book. Stop there.

options.label: Honestly, it looks like how my head feels

insight.reveal: People who choose this often notice that their space and their mood move together. The intriguing part: the link runs both ways, so a small change on the table can sometimes lift a cloudy day a little.
insight.step: On your next heavy day, clear one small surface and check if your mood shifts, even slightly.

questions.prompt: When do you usually start a new habit?

options.label: On a Monday or the first of the month

insight.reveal: People who choose fresh starts like a clean line between the old self and the new one. The hidden cost: if the line is missed, the next start can feel a week or a month away.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Pick one small habit and start it on an ordinary day this week, like a Thursday.

options.label: Right now, the moment the idea hits

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests energy is your fuel more than planning. People like this often start many things with joy, and the ones that last are usually the ones tied to something they already do every day.
insight.step: Attach one new habit to something you already do daily: 'After I make tea, I will…'

options.label: After I find the best way to do it

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who want to start right more than start soon. The same pattern tends to show up when buying things: lots of reading reviews, then a long pause before choosing.
insight.step: This week, start one habit with the 'good enough' method, then improve it after three days.

options.label: I keep planning it but rarely begin

insight.reveal: People who choose this often enjoy the planned self a lot. Planning feels like progress, so the brain gets a small reward without the hard part. The missing piece is usually not motivation, it's a clear trigger.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Write a when-then plan for one habit: 'When I sit down after dinner, I will…'

questions.prompt: You're stuck waiting in a line for ten minutes. What do you do?

options.label: Watch the people around me

insight.reveal: People who watch others in lines often collect small stories without noticing. They tend to be good at reading a room fast, and are often the first to sense when a friend's mood is off.
insight.step: Next time you wait, guess one stranger's day from small clues. Just for fun.

options.label: Scroll on my phone

insight.reveal: Your choice is common, but here's the twist: people who fill every gap with a screen often say their mind feels 'full' at night. The gaps were where the mind used to tidy itself.
insight.step: In your next line, leave the phone in your pocket for the first two minutes.

options.label: Make plans or lists in my head

insight.reveal: This answer suggests idle time feels like wasted time to you. People like this are often the ones who remember birthdays and deadlines, and find it hard to switch off on holiday.
insight.step: Next time you wait, try to notice five sounds instead of making a plan.

options.label: Get restless and annoyed the whole time

insight.reveal: People who feel this often aren't impatient people overall; they're people with full days. The irritation is usually less about the line and more about losing control of time.
insight.step: Next time you're stuck, decide on purpose what the ten minutes are for. See if choosing it changes the feeling.

questions.prompt: How do you keep track of things you need to do?

options.label: A written or phone list I really use

insight.reveal: People who trust a list often have quieter heads, because the list holds what the mind would keep repeating. The same people often sleep a little easier on busy weeks.
insight.step: Tonight, add one thing that's been on your mind to your list and see if it stops repeating.

options.label: I keep it all in my head

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you trust your memory and enjoy freedom from systems. The hidden pattern: people who do this often remember the big things perfectly and the tiny ones at 2am.
insight.step: For three days, write down only the tiny tasks. Keep the big ones in your head as usual.

options.label: I write lists, then lose them

insight.reveal: People who choose this often get the benefit from writing, not from reading. Making the list calms the mind, so the list has done its job before it's even lost.
insight.step: Write tomorrow's list somewhere you'll see it by accident, like your phone's lock screen.

options.label: I add things I already did, just to tick them

insight.reveal: This answer tends to belong to people who need proof of a day well spent. Ticking done things is a quiet way of telling yourself 'I was enough today', and many people secretly do it.
insight.step: Tonight, write three things you did today that were never on any list.

questions.prompt: A free Saturday with no plans. By noon you've usually…

options.label: Done chores and errands

insight.reveal: People who choose this often need the 'should' things done before fun feels allowed. The same rule tends to show up at work: you clear the boring tasks first, even when the fun one matters more.
insight.step: Next free day, do one fun thing before any chore. Notice whether the fun feels earned or stolen.

options.label: Gone somewhere new

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests empty time feels like an invitation. People like this often remember their year by places, not dates, and a week with no new sights can feel oddly long.
insight.step: This week, take a different route to somewhere you go often.

options.label: Done nothing, and loved it

insight.reveal: People who can truly enjoy doing nothing often recover faster from busy weeks. It's a skill more than a lazy habit, and those who have it often find guilt-free rest hard to explain to others.
insight.step: Protect one hour this weekend with nothing in it. Tell someone it's a plan.

options.label: Done nothing, and felt guilty about it

insight.reveal: This answer often shows a mind that measures days by output. The surprise: the guilt usually takes more energy than the rest gave back, so you end the day tired from resting.
insight.step: Next time you rest, give it a name in advance, like 'recharging time', and see if the guilt shrinks.

questions.prompt: At a café or restaurant you love, you usually order…

options.label: The same thing every time

insight.reveal: People who always order the same thing often save their decision energy for things that matter more to them. The same people tend to have a small number of very old friends.
insight.step: Next visit, try one new item, but keep your favourite on the side as a safety net.

options.label: Something new each time

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests that for you, a small risk is part of the fun. People like this often enjoy travel planning and get restless when weeks look the same.
insight.step: This week, bring the 'something new' rule to a different place, like the route home or a song.

options.label: Whatever the person with me gets

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who like to keep things smooth and shared. The hidden pattern: the same people sometimes forget what they themselves wanted, in bigger choices too.
insight.step: Next time you eat out, decide your order before anyone else speaks.

options.label: I change my mind at the very last second

insight.reveal: People who switch at the last second often pick by gut, then let doubt argue. The intriguing part: the first choice is often the one they actually wanted, and the switch is about avoiding regret.
insight.step: Next time you order, keep your first choice and see if you enjoy it more.

questions.prompt: How many books, shows or projects do you have half-finished?

options.label: None, I finish what I start

insight.reveal: People who finish everything often feel a quiet pull from open loops. The twist: some also keep going with things they no longer enjoy, because stopping feels like losing.
insight.step: Choose one thing you're finishing out of duty, and give yourself permission to stop.

options.label: A couple, that's normal

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests a healthy balance between curiosity and follow-through. People like this often finish what they love and let the rest go without much drama.
insight.step: This week, finish one small thing you're close to the end of.

options.label: Lots, I love starting things

insight.reveal: People who choose this often get their joy from the beginning, when everything is new. The same pattern can show up in friendships: easy, warm starts and many people you'd love to see again.
insight.step: Pick one half-finished thing and do just one more step of it this week.

options.label: Lots, and they quietly weigh on me

insight.reveal: This answer tends to belong to people who carry their unfinished things like small stones in a bag. Interestingly, deciding to officially stop something often lifts the weight as much as finishing it.
insight.step: Choose one unfinished thing and officially end it today. Say 'done' out loud.

questions.prompt: You promised yourself one small thing today. By evening…

options.label: It's done

insight.reveal: People who keep small promises to themselves often trust themselves with bigger ones. That self-trust tends to make hard decisions feel less scary.
insight.step: Tomorrow, make yourself one tiny promise and keep it on purpose.

options.label: It's moved to tomorrow

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests 'tomorrow' is a place where many good intentions wait. People like this are often realistic about today's energy, but tomorrow's self gets the heavy bag.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Next time you move something to tomorrow, decide the exact time you'll do it.

options.label: I forgot until right now

insight.reveal: People who choose this often make promises to themselves silently, without any reminder. Promises to others get written down; promises to yourself live only in your head, so they slip.
insight.step: Write one promise to yourself in the same place you write promises to others.

options.label: I skipped it, but I kept every promise to others

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people who are deeply reliable for everyone except themselves. The pattern is common in caring people: your own needs go to the bottom of the list without a sound.
insight.step: This week, treat one promise to yourself like a meeting with someone you respect.

questions.prompt: What usually tells you it's time to go to sleep?

options.label: The clock: it's my usual time

insight.reveal: People who sleep by the clock often like days with a clear shape. The same people tend to feel a bit lost on holidays, when the shape disappears.
insight.step: On your next free night, keep your usual bedtime and notice how the next morning feels.

options.label: My body: I just feel tired

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you listen to your body's signals. People who do this often notice hunger, stress and tiredness early, before they turn into a bad mood.
insight.step: Tonight, notice the very first sign of tiredness, like slow blinking, and go then.

options.label: The show or video finally ends

insight.reveal: This answer tends to mean the screen decides bedtime, not you. People who sleep this way often say they 'lose' the last hour of the day without remembering what filled it.
insight.step: Tonight, choose your stopping point before you press play.

options.label: Nothing, I stop when I can't stay awake

insight.reveal: People who choose this often hold on to night because it's the only time that feels truly theirs. Going to bed can feel like handing the day back to everyone else.
insight.step: Tomorrow, find 20 minutes of 'my time' earlier in the day, then see if bedtime is easier.

questions.prompt: It's late, you're tired, and it's your first free moment all day. You…

options.label: Go to bed anyway

insight.reveal: People who choose sleep over free time often think of tomorrow's self as a real person to look after. That same care for 'future me' tends to show up in how they plan meals and money.
insight.step: This week, find a small free moment earlier in the day so night isn't the only one.

options.label: Stay up a little to enjoy it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you know you need both rest and something just for you. People like this usually manage the trade well, as long as 'a little' has a clear end.
insight.step: Tonight, set a gentle alarm for when 'a little' is over.

options.label: Stay up far too late scrolling

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people whose days are full of other people's needs. Staying up becomes a way to take time back. The catch: scrolling is rarely the thing you actually wanted to do with it.
insight.research: People with stronger present bias, preferring smaller rewards now over bigger ones later, are more likely to carry credit card debt.
insight.step: Tonight, ask: 'What would I really enjoy for 20 minutes?' Then do that instead of scrolling.

options.label: Stay up because sleeping makes tomorrow come faster

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel the next day as something heavy waiting at the door. Staying awake feels like holding the door shut. The pattern usually points to one specific thing about tomorrow, not all of it.
insight.step: Tonight, name the one part of tomorrow you're dreading, then write the first small step for it.

questions.prompt: It's mid-afternoon and your energy drops. You reach for…

options.label: A short walk or a glass of water

insight.reveal: People who answer a slump with movement often treat energy like a battery to recharge, not a fire to feed. The same people tend to deal with bad moods by changing the room.
insight.step: Tomorrow, when the slump hits, step outside for three minutes and see what changes.

options.label: Coffee or tea

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests the slump is a ritual as much as a need. Interestingly, many people say the break around the cup helps as much as the drink itself.
insight.step: Next slump, take the break without the drink once and compare how you feel.

options.label: Something sweet

insight.reveal: This answer often shows a quick-reward brain at a tired moment. People who reach for sweets in the afternoon often skipped something earlier, like lunch, water, or a few minutes away from the screen.
insight.step: Tomorrow, notice what you skipped before the slump. Fix that one thing.

options.label: I push through and feel annoyed at my body

insight.reveal: People who choose this often treat their body like an employee who should keep up. The twist: the ones who push hardest are usually the ones with the most to do, and the least permission to pause.
insight.step: Next slump, give yourself a five-minute break and call it work, because it is.

questions.prompt: On a stressful day, the way you eat…

options.label: Doesn't really change

insight.reveal: People whose eating stays steady under stress often have one fixed anchor in their routine. That anchor tends to keep other things steady too, like sleep and mood.
insight.step: On your next busy day, notice which part of your routine stayed the same. Keep it.

options.label: I forget to eat

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests stress narrows your focus to the task until everything else disappears. People like this are often great in a crisis and surprised later by how tired they feel.
insight.step: Tomorrow, set one reminder for a real meal break, even if the day is calm.

options.label: I snack more without noticing

insight.reveal: This answer often means your hands look for comfort while your mind is busy. People who notice this usually find the snacking happens at one exact moment, like after a certain message or meeting.
insight.step: Next stressful day, notice the exact moment you first reach for a snack.

options.label: I eat to feel calmer, and I know it

insight.reveal: People who choose this are often more honest with themselves than most. Knowing why you eat is a real skill. The next step for people like this is usually adding one more calming option, not removing food.
insight.step: Next time you reach for calm, try one other calming thing first, like a song, then decide.

questions.prompt: When you move your body, it's mostly because…

options.label: I enjoy it

insight.reveal: People who move for fun often stay active for years, because it never feels like a task. The same people tend to pick hobbies by feeling, not by results.
insight.step: This week, try one new way to move just for fun, like dancing in the kitchen.

options.label: It's how I get places

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests movement is built into your life, not added to it. People like this often do more than they think, because built-in movement rarely gets counted.
insight.step: Tomorrow, take the slightly longer way somewhere and notice how it feels.

options.label: I'd feel guilty if I didn't

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from a strong inner rule-keeper. People who move from guilt are usually very consistent, but they tend to miss the moments when it could feel good.
insight.step: Next time you move, pick the version you'd enjoy most, not the one you 'should' do.

options.label: To burn off feelings I can't name

insight.reveal: People who choose this often understand their feelings through their body first, words later. Many find that after moving, the feeling finally has a name.
insight.step: After your next walk or workout, ask yourself one question: 'What was I carrying?'

questions.prompt: You pick up your phone for no reason. What do you open first?

options.label: Messages

insight.reveal: People who check messages first often feel most at ease knowing the people around them are okay. The same instinct tends to make them quick to reply and slow to leave a group chat.
insight.step: Next time you open messages, reply to one person you've been meaning to answer.

options.label: News

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you like to be ready for whatever is happening. People who check news by reflex are often the planners in their group, and the ones who feel world events in their body.
insight.step: Tomorrow, choose two set times to check the news, and skip it in between.

options.label: A social feed

insight.reveal: People who reach for a feed often want a small spark of something new. The hidden pattern: the reach usually happens right after a boring or hard moment, as a tiny escape.
insight.step: Next time you open a feed, notice what you were doing right before.

options.label: Nothing, I unlock it, look, and lock it again

insight.reveal: This answer is more revealing than it seems. Unlocking with no goal often means the hand is looking for relief, not information. People who notice this often find a feeling, like boredom or worry, right underneath.
insight.step: Next time you unlock with no reason, name the feeling you have in one word.

questions.prompt: On days with nothing planned, you wake up…

options.label: At my usual time

insight.reveal: People whose body wakes at the same time every day often feel more even through the week. They also tend to be the ones enjoying a quiet hour while the house sleeps.
insight.step: On your next free morning, use the early quiet hour for something just for you.

options.label: A bit later than usual

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests a body that enjoys a little extra but doesn't go wild. People like this often handle change well because their rhythm bends without breaking.
insight.step: This week, notice which morning you feel best, and what you did the night before.

options.label: Much later, I'm catching up

insight.reveal: This answer often means your week borrows sleep that the weekend pays back. People who sleep in a lot often feel a slow, foggy Monday, like coming back from another time zone.
insight.step: This week, go to bed 15 minutes earlier on two weeknights and see if the weekend changes.

options.label: Earlier, I don't want to waste free time

insight.reveal: People who wake early on free days often feel time slipping away. The twist: the fear of wasting the day can make it feel shorter, not longer.
insight.step: Next free morning, stay in bed five extra minutes on purpose, and call it part of the plan.

questions.prompt: When you finally sit on the sofa to rest, you feel…

options.label: Relaxed right away

insight.reveal: People who relax fast often have an easy 'off switch' between work and home. Others around them may even calm down a little just by being near them.
insight.step: This week, share your rest with someone else for ten minutes, no screens.

options.label: Relaxed, after a while

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests your mind needs a short landing time. People like this often find that one small ritual, like changing clothes, makes the landing faster.
insight.step: Next time you get home, try one small 'landing' ritual and see if rest comes sooner.

options.label: Like I should be doing something

insight.reveal: People who choose this often believe rest must be earned. The hidden pattern: they rarely feel the day has earned it, so rest keeps getting postponed.
insight.step: Next time you sit down, tell yourself: 'This is on the list too.'

options.label: Rested body, busy mind

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people whose thoughts get loud only when the room gets quiet. The busy mind isn't a failure to rest; it's usually the first moment there's space to think.
insight.step: Before you sit down, spend two minutes writing what's on your mind, then rest.

questions.prompt: How do you usually decide when to eat?

options.label: When I feel hungry

insight.reveal: People who eat by hunger often trust their body's signals in other ways too, like knowing when to rest or when a place feels wrong.
insight.step: Tomorrow, before each meal, pause and ask: 'Am I a little hungry, or very hungry?'

options.label: At fixed times

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests routine gives you calm. People who eat at set times often like knowing what comes next, and a late meal can throw off their whole evening.
insight.step: This week, try one meal slightly off schedule and notice how it feels.

options.label: When someone else is eating

insight.reveal: This answer often means food is social for you more than practical. People like this tend to eat better with company and forget meals completely when alone.
insight.step: Next time you eat alone, make it feel like a small event: a plate, a seat, no screen.

options.label: When I notice I'm cranky and it's been hours

insight.reveal: People who choose this often get so absorbed that the body's quiet signals get ignored until they're loud. The bad mood is often the first signal they notice.
insight.step: Tomorrow, set one gentle reminder halfway through your busiest stretch to check if you're hungry.

questions.prompt: You wake at 3am and can't fall back asleep. Your mind goes to…

options.label: Nothing much, I drift off again

insight.reveal: People who drift back easily often leave the day's problems at the door. The same people tend to forgive small slights fast, because they don't replay them.
insight.step: Next time you wake at night, notice what helped you drift, and remember it.

options.label: Small tasks for tomorrow

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests your mind keeps working the list while you sleep. People like this often find that a notepad by the bed ends the night shift.
insight.step: Keep paper by your bed tonight. If tasks wake you, write them down and close the shop.

options.label: Big questions about my life

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who rarely give big questions room during the day, so they arrive at night. The questions are real, but 3am is the worst time to answer them.
insight.step: This week, give one big question ten minutes in daylight, on a walk.

options.label: Something embarrassing from years ago

insight.reveal: People who choose this often have a vivid memory for social moments. The twist: the people in those memories almost never remember them; you are the only one still keeping that file.
insight.step: Next time an old moment returns, ask: 'Would anyone else remember this?' Then let it go.

questions.prompt: Payday arrives. What goes first?

options.label: Bills

insight.reveal: People who pay bills first often feel calm only after the 'must' list is clear. The same rule tends to show up in how they eat a meal: the vegetables before the best part.
insight.step: On the next payday, do one small nice thing on the same day, right after the bills.

options.label: Putting some aside first

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you treat future you as someone who deserves a share. People like this often find it easy to wait for good things, and sometimes hard to enjoy them once they come.
insight.step: This month, set aside a small amount just for enjoying, and actually spend it.

options.label: Checking my balance again and again

insight.reveal: People who check over and over on payday are often looking for a feeling, not a number: the feeling of being safe. The relief usually lasts only until the next check.
insight.step: On the next payday, check once, then put the phone down for the rest of the day.

options.label: Something for me, then I worry about the rest later

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people who work hard and want the work to feel worth it right away. The pattern: the joy is real, but the worry later can take more from you than the treat gave.
insight.research: People with stronger present bias, preferring smaller rewards now over bigger ones later, are more likely to carry credit card debt.
insight.step: Next payday, decide your treat before the money arrives, so it's a plan, not a reaction.

questions.prompt: A friend asks to borrow some money. You…

options.label: Lend it and expect it back

insight.reveal: People who lend with clear terms tend to keep friendships cleaner over time. Clear rules make it easier to say yes, because nobody has to guess.
insight.step: Next time someone owes you, mention it kindly within a week instead of waiting.

options.label: Give it and don't expect it back

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you see money between friends as a gift, not a loan. People like this often avoid a lot of awkwardness, and some quietly limit how much they give so it never hurts.
insight.step: This week, notice if there's anyone you give to who never asks how you're doing.

options.label: Say no politely

insight.reveal: People who say no to lending often protect friendships by keeping money out of them. The hidden pattern: they're often generous in other ways, like time or help.
insight.step: Next time you say no, offer one other kind of help instead, if you want to.

options.label: Lend it, then feel too awkward to ask for it back

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who fear that asking will cost the friendship. The irony: the silence usually hurts the friendship more than one clear question would.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Practise one kind sentence for asking back, like 'Hey, whenever you can, no rush.'

questions.prompt: Dinner with friends ends. How do you split the bill?

options.label: Split it equally

insight.reveal: People who split equally often value the evening over the maths. The same people tend to dislike scorekeeping in friendships, and notice quickly when someone else keeps score.
insight.step: Next dinner, notice how the group decides to split. Who leads it?

options.label: Everyone pays exactly for what they had

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests fairness means precision to you. People like this are often trusted with group money, and sometimes feel quietly taken advantage of by the 'let's just split it' crowd.
insight.step: Next time, try splitting equally once and see if it feels as bad as expected.

options.label: I quietly put in more than my share

insight.reveal: People who quietly overpay often get real joy from it, as long as nobody notices. It may be one of the cheapest ways to feel good.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: Next time you treat someone, notice how long the good feeling lasts.

options.label: I offer to pay for everyone, then regret it

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from a strong wish to be the warm one in the group. The regret later usually isn't about money; it's about wondering whether anyone noticed or would do the same.
insight.step: Next time you feel the urge to pay for all, wait ten seconds before saying it.

questions.prompt: You see something you love but didn't plan to buy. You…

options.label: Walk away

insight.reveal: People who can walk away often find the wanting fades within hours. Their secret is usually not willpower; it's that they don't picture owning it before they leave.
insight.step: Next time you walk away, check in two days if you still think about it.

options.label: Wait a day and see if I still want it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you trust tomorrow's version of you to judge better. People who use a waiting rule tend to regret purchases less, and enjoy the ones they make more.
insight.step: Make a 'wait one day' list on your phone this week for things you want.

options.label: Buy it right away

insight.reveal: People who buy on the spot often enjoy the hunt as much as the item. The pattern: the best feeling is usually at checkout, and it fades faster than the item stays.
insight.research: People with stronger present bias, preferring smaller rewards now over bigger ones later, are more likely to carry credit card debt.
insight.step: Next time you want to buy on the spot, take a photo first and decide in an hour.

options.label: Buy it and don't tell anyone

insight.reveal: This answer often shows a quiet conflict between wanting and being seen wanting. People who hide purchases usually aren't hiding the item; they're avoiding a judgement they already make of themselves.
insight.step: Next time you buy something for you, tell one person about it plainly and see how it feels.

questions.prompt: You get an unexpected bit of extra money. Where does it go?

options.label: Into savings

insight.reveal: People who save surprise money often feel safety as a kind of pleasure. The same people tend to keep spare batteries, extra snacks, and a plan B for most things.
insight.step: Next time, keep a tiny part of any surprise money for something fun.

options.label: A trip, a meal out, an experience

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you buy memories more than things. People who do this often retell those moments for years, and each retelling seems to add to the value.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: This month, plan one small experience and tell someone the story afterward.

options.label: A gift or treat for someone else

insight.reveal: People who spend surprise money on others often feel richer from giving than from getting. The joy tends to last longer when the gift is a surprise.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: This week, do one small surprise for someone, even something free.

options.label: It just disappears, I'm not sure where

insight.reveal: This answer is honest and very common. Surprise money often feels like 'not real money', so it slips into small spends. The pattern says more about labels than about carelessness.
insight.step: Next time extra money arrives, give it a name, like 'shoe money', before you spend any.

questions.prompt: How often do you look at your account balance?

options.label: About once a week

insight.reveal: People who check weekly often treat money like weather: worth a look, not worth a worry. The same calm tends to show up in how they read messages and news.
insight.step: This week, notice how you feel right before your check. Calm, or bracing?

options.label: Every day

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you like small updates more than big surprises. People who check daily often catch problems early, and sometimes feel small dips more than they need to.
insight.step: Try skipping one day this week and see if anything changes.

options.label: Only when I really have to

insight.reveal: People who avoid the balance often aren't careless; they're protecting their mood. The twist: not knowing usually feels worse than the real number.
insight.step: Pick one quiet moment this week, with a drink you like, and check once.

options.label: Many times a day, even when nothing changed

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people for whom money means safety, not just spending. The checking brings a moment of relief, and the relief is what keeps the loop going.
insight.step: For one day, check only at lunch and at night. Notice what you feel instead.

questions.prompt: Something you bought goes on sale the next day. You…

options.label: Shrug, it's fine

insight.reveal: People who shrug at price drops often judge a purchase by whether they like it, not by the deal. They tend to enjoy what they own more as a result.
insight.step: This week, notice one thing you own that you love, regardless of what it cost.

options.label: Go and get the difference back

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you like things to be fair and correct. People like this often enjoy small wins and handle forms and phone calls better than most.
insight.step: Next time you fix a small unfairness, notice how good it feels, and why.

options.label: Feel annoyed for days

insight.reveal: People who stay annoyed often aren't upset about the money; they're upset about having been 'caught out'. The same feeling can show up after giving a wrong answer in public.
insight.research: People who vented anger while dwelling on the person who annoyed them became angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing.
insight.step: Next time you feel caught out, give the feeling one sentence, then change the subject.

options.label: Feel like I always pay too much

insight.reveal: This answer often hides a bigger story: 'things don't work out for me'. People who notice this story in small moments can often catch it in bigger ones too.
insight.step: This week, write down one time things did work out for you, however small.

questions.prompt: Someone asks how much you earn. You…

options.label: Just tell them

insight.reveal: People who share openly often think secrets give money more power than it deserves. The same openness tends to make others trust them with their own worries.
insight.step: This week, notice whether anyone opens up to you after you're open first.

options.label: Give a vague answer

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you protect your privacy without making it awkward. People like this are often skilled at small talk and rarely let others see what they really think.
insight.step: Next time you're vague, notice whether it's about privacy or about being compared.

options.label: Change the subject

insight.reveal: People who change the subject often keep money in a locked room, even from close friends. It can be a sign of strong privacy, or of feelings about money that never got words.
insight.step: Ask yourself privately this week: what feeling shows up when someone asks about money?

options.label: Feel judged, even if they just asked

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who measure themselves before anyone else can. The judgement usually comes from inside, and most people asking are just curious.
insight.step: Next time someone asks a money question, assume curiosity first and see if it changes the feeling.

questions.prompt: How much money would feel like 'enough'?

options.label: About what I have now

insight.reveal: People who feel they have enough often measure life by time and people, not things. The same people tend to say yes to slower jobs and longer lunches.
insight.step: This week, use some of your 'enough' feeling to give someone your time.

options.label: A bit more than now

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests a clear, reachable goal. People who want 'a bit more' often know exactly what it would change, like less stress around one bill or one trip.
insight.research: For most people, happiness keeps rising with income; for the least happy group, it stops rising above a fairly high income.
insight.step: Name the one thing 'a bit more' would change. Is there a small step toward it this week?

options.label: I keep moving the line

insight.reveal: People who keep moving the line often adapt fast to new comfort. It helps them aim high, but the finish line keeps walking away just as they reach it.
insight.step: Write down one thing you once wanted badly and now have. Look at it for a moment.

options.label: I'm not sure any amount would feel safe

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people for whom money is a shield, not a tool. The feeling is usually older than the bank account, and no number fully calms it.
insight.step: This week, notice one moment when you felt safe that had nothing to do with money.

questions.prompt: Choosing a gift for someone close, you usually…

options.label: Ask them what they want

insight.reveal: People who ask often care most that the gift is used. The hidden pattern: they tend to prefer clear requests in relationships too, not guessing games.
insight.step: Next gift, ask what they want, then add one small surprise.

options.label: Get something practical

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you show care through usefulness. People like this are often the friend who fixes things, lends tools and remembers what someone ran out of.
insight.step: This week, notice what someone close keeps running out of.

options.label: Find something they'd never buy themselves

insight.reveal: People who choose this often study the people they love. They notice small wishes said in passing, and remember them months later.
insight.step: This week, listen for one small wish someone mentions, and save it in your phone.

options.label: Spend more than I should, to show I care

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from a worry that care must be visible to count. The surprise: most people remember how thoughtful a gift felt, not what it cost.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: Next gift, add a short handwritten note and spend a little less. Watch the reaction.

questions.prompt: How do you start your working day?

options.label: With the most important task

insight.reveal: People who start with the big task often feel the rest of the day is a bonus. The same people tend to eat the food they like least on the plate first.
insight.step: Tomorrow, decide your first task tonight, so the morning starts without choosing.

options.label: Clearing messages

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests other people's needs set the start of your day. People like this are often very responsive, and sometimes reach lunch without touching their own work.
insight.step: Tomorrow, do 20 minutes of your own work before opening messages.

options.label: A small, easy task to warm up

insight.reveal: People who warm up first often know that starting is the hardest part. The pattern is clever, as long as the warm-up doesn't quietly become the whole morning.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Tomorrow, set a limit: one warm-up task, then the real one.

options.label: Rereading what I sent yesterday

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who care deeply about how they come across. Rereading can feel like checking, but it usually feeds doubt more than it fixes errors.
insight.step: Tomorrow, skip the rereading once. If something was wrong, someone will tell you.

questions.prompt: Your boss sends: 'Can we talk later?' You…

options.label: Think nothing of it

insight.reveal: People who stay calm with vague messages often assume good intent by default. That trust tends to make them easier to work with, and less tired at the end of the day.
insight.step: Next time you send a vague message, add one word of context. Others may not be as calm.

options.label: Ask what it's about

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you'd rather know than wonder. People like this often handle bad news well, but find waiting harder than the news itself.
insight.step: Next time you're waiting on something, plan one small task to fill the gap.

options.label: Start preparing for every possible topic

insight.reveal: People who prepare for everything often turn worry into action. It works, but the preparation can quietly double the stress of a simple chat.
insight.step: Next time, prepare for only the one most likely topic and see if it's enough.

options.label: Imagine the worst until we talk

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people who read silence as a sign of trouble. The same pattern can show up when a friend replies slowly. Most of the time the 'later' talk is about something small.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time you imagine the worst, also imagine the most boring possible reason.

questions.prompt: A colleague presents your idea as theirs. You…

options.label: Mention it calmly to them later

insight.reveal: People who choose this often protect both the work and the relationship. They tend to be trusted as fair, and quietly remembered by people who saw what happened.
insight.step: Practise one calm sentence for next time, like: 'Glad that idea from our chat landed well.'

options.label: Speak up right there

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests fairness matters more to you than comfort. People like this often become the person others go to when something isn't right.
insight.step: Next time you speak up, add one generous word for the other person too.

options.label: Say nothing, and feel it for weeks

insight.reveal: People who choose this often replay the moment, finding the perfect reply too late. The replaying tends to keep the anger warm rather than letting it go.
insight.research: People who vented anger while dwelling on the person who annoyed them became angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing.
insight.step: Next time, say one short true sentence soon, even if imperfect, instead of the perfect one never.

options.label: Say nothing, but quietly trust them less forever

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who protect themselves by stepping back instead of stepping in. The other person may never know why things changed.
insight.step: Think of one person you quietly trust less. Is there one small thing they could do to win it back?

questions.prompt: If pay didn't matter, would you keep doing your kind of work?

options.label: Yes, I'd keep doing it

insight.reveal: People who'd keep their work often find meaning in the small daily parts, not only the results. They tend to talk about work stories at dinner without being asked.
insight.step: This week, notice which part of your work you'd do even for free.

options.label: Something close to it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you like your field but not your exact spot in it. People like this often have a 'side' version of their work they think about on long trips.
insight.step: Spend ten minutes this week looking at what that nearby version looks like day to day.

options.label: Something completely different

insight.reveal: People who choose this often carry a second life in their head. The interesting part: that second life usually shows up already in their hobbies.
insight.step: Look at how you spent your last free weekend. Is the other life already there?

options.label: I've never let myself really answer that

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people who have been practical for a long time, maybe for others. The question feels risky because a real answer might ask something of you.
insight.step: Let yourself answer the question for one minute this week, with no plan to act on it.

questions.prompt: Your work gets praised in front of others. You…

options.label: Say thank you and enjoy it

insight.reveal: People who simply accept praise often make others feel good about giving it. The same people are usually generous with praise themselves.
insight.step: This week, praise one specific thing a colleague did, in front of others.

options.label: Pass the credit to the team

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you see work as shared. People like this are often loved by teams, but sometimes forgotten when big chances come around.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Next time, say 'thank you' first, then mention the team.

options.label: Downplay it: 'It was nothing'

insight.reveal: People who downplay praise often feel visible in a way that's uncomfortable. The hidden cost: others may start to believe the work really was nothing.
insight.step: Next time you're praised, say only 'Thank you, I worked hard on it.' Nothing else.

options.label: Enjoy it, then wonder if they meant it

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who trust criticism more than praise. Interestingly, others often judge your abilities more clearly than you do.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.
insight.step: Write down one piece of praise you got this month and keep it where you'll see it.

questions.prompt: You find a mistake of yours that nobody has noticed. You…

options.label: Fix it and tell the people affected

insight.reveal: People who fix and tell often build trust that lasts years. Their colleagues tend to believe their good news more, because they share bad news too.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: This week, notice someone else owning a mistake and thank them for it.

options.label: Fix it quietly

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you care about the result more than the story. People like this tend to be reliable, and sometimes their careful saves go completely unseen.
insight.step: Next time you fix something quietly, tell one person. Not to confess, just so your care is seen.

options.label: Wait to see if anyone notices

insight.reveal: People who choose this often aren't hiding; they're hoping it will fix itself. The waiting tends to feel worse over time, and the mistake grows heavier than it was.
insight.step: Pick one small open mistake and close it this week, even quietly.

options.label: Lose sleep deciding what to do

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people with high standards and a loud inner judge. The deciding usually takes far more energy than the fix would.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Next time, give yourself ten minutes to decide, then act on whatever you choose.

questions.prompt: A big task is due in a week. When do you really start?

options.label: Today

insight.reveal: People who start right away often hate the feeling of something hanging over them. The same instinct tends to make them answer hard messages first.
insight.step: This week, notice if starting early ever leads you to do more than was needed.

options.label: Mid-week, with a plan

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you work best with a little pressure and a clear map. People like this tend to know their own speed very well.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: For your next task, write the plan as when-then steps and see if it runs smoother.

options.label: The night before

insight.reveal: People who start at the last minute often do their best thinking under pressure. The hidden cost is usually not the quality; it's the week of low-level worry before it.
insight.step: Next big task, do just ten minutes on day one. Only ten. Then stop.

options.label: Early, but then I redo it many times

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who start fast and find it hard to stop. The early start is diligence; the endless redoing is often worry dressed up as care.
insight.step: Next task, decide in advance how many drafts you'll allow yourself. Then stop at that number.

questions.prompt: In a meeting, you have an idea. You…

options.label: Say it right away

insight.reveal: People who speak up fast often think out loud; the idea gets better as they say it. Others may find it inspiring, or occasionally hard to keep up with.
insight.step: Next meeting, ask one quieter person what they think before you speak.

options.label: Wait for the right moment

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you care about timing and fit. People like this often say fewer things that land better, but sometimes the right moment never comes.
insight.step: Next meeting, set a rule: if the moment hasn't come by halfway, make it.

options.label: Tell one person after the meeting

insight.reveal: People who share ideas afterward often think best one-to-one. Their ideas tend to reach the room later, sometimes in someone else's voice.
insight.step: Next time, send your idea in writing to the whole group within an hour.

options.label: Stay quiet, then hear someone else say it

insight.reveal: This answer often comes with a mix of 'I knew it!' and quiet frustration. The good news is hidden in the pain: your instinct was right, which is worth trusting next time.
insight.step: Next meeting, say your idea as a question: 'What if we tried…?' It feels less risky.

questions.prompt: Where do you want to be at work in five years?

options.label: I have a clear target

insight.reveal: People with clear targets often feel calm because the next step is obvious. The twist: they sometimes don't notice good doors opening off to the side.
insight.step: This week, ask someone in a different role what they love about their work.

options.label: Just better at what I do

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you care about craft more than titles. People like this often become the quiet expert everyone goes to, sometimes without a title to match.
insight.step: Pick one small skill to improve this week and practise it for ten minutes a day.

options.label: Free to choose my own hours and work

insight.reveal: People who choose freedom often value control more than money or status. The same need tends to show up at home, like wanting your own corner or your own plans.
insight.step: This week, choose one small part of your work and do it exactly the way you like.

options.label: I'm afraid to want too much

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who've learned that hoping can hurt. The careful wanting protects you, but it can also keep your real goal unspoken, even to yourself.
insight.step: Write your 'too much' goal on paper, just once, and keep it private.

questions.prompt: Colleagues invite you to lunch. You…

options.label: Join happily

insight.reveal: People who join easily often build trust through small, regular moments. These small lunches tend to matter more over the years than any team event.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: This week, invite someone you rarely talk to.

options.label: Join sometimes, not always

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you balance people time and quiet time well. People like this often pick lunches by who is going, not by habit.
insight.step: Next time you say no, suggest a different day so the door stays open.

options.label: Eat alone to recharge

insight.reveal: People who eat alone often protect their energy so they can be fully present later. Others may read it as distance, even when it's the opposite.
insight.step: This week, join once for a short coffee instead of a full lunch.

options.label: Join, but feel like an outsider

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people who notice every small sign of belonging or not. The surprise: others at the table are often feeling the same way.
insight.step: Next lunch, ask one person a question about their life outside work.

questions.prompt: How do you learn to use a new app or gadget?

options.label: Read the guide or watch a tutorial

insight.reveal: People who learn from the guide often like to understand the whole before touching the parts. The same people tend to read the full menu before ordering.
insight.step: Next new tool, try pressing buttons for two minutes before reading anything.

options.label: Just press buttons until it works

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you learn by doing and don't fear breaking things. People like this are often the ones friends call to 'fix the thing'.
insight.step: Next time, teach someone else the shortcut you found.

options.label: Ask someone to show me

insight.reveal: People who learn by asking often remember the person as much as the steps. Learning becomes social, and the knowledge sticks better.
insight.step: This week, ask someone to show you one thing they're good at.

options.label: Avoid it until I really have to

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who've felt slow with tech before and don't want to feel it again. The fear is usually bigger than the learning turns out to be.
insight.step: Pick one feature you've been avoiding and spend five minutes on it.

questions.prompt: Halfway through an argument, you realise you're wrong. You…

options.label: Say so right away

insight.reveal: People who admit mistakes quickly often win more trust than people who win arguments. Others tend to believe them more next time they say they're sure.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: This week, say 'I was wrong about that' out loud once, even about something tiny.

options.label: Admit it later, when things are calm

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you need a little space before you can bend. People like this tend to make peace well, but the other person may spend the gap feeling unheard.
insight.step: Next time, say 'You might be right, let me think' in the moment. It buys time kindly.

options.label: Quietly change the subject

insight.reveal: People who change the subject often feel being wrong in public as a small loss of face. The idea usually still changes inside them, just without anyone seeing.
insight.step: Next time, try a tiny admission like 'Good point.' Notice how little it costs.

options.label: Keep defending it, then think about it all night

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people whose pride and honesty argue with each other. The night thinking is a sign the honest side is winning, just late.
insight.step: Next time you can't stop thinking about it, send a short 'You were right' message the next day.

questions.prompt: You look up one quick fact. An hour later you're…

options.label: Long done, I got the fact

insight.reveal: People who stop at the fact often have strong focus and a clear sense of purpose. They're rarely lost online, and sometimes miss happy accidents.
insight.step: This week, allow yourself one 15-minute wander after a search.

options.label: Deep in five related articles

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests curiosity pulls you down, layer by layer. People like this often become quiet experts in odd topics, and love telling others what they found.
insight.step: Tell one person the most surprising thing you learned this week.

options.label: Learning something totally unrelated

insight.reveal: People who end up somewhere unrelated often have a mind that links distant ideas. That same jumping is often where their most creative ideas come from.
insight.step: Next time you wander, write down where you started and where you ended.

options.label: Feeling like I know less than before

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who see how big a topic really is. Feeling you know less is often a sign you understand more.
insight.step: Next time you feel lost in a topic, write three things you now know that you didn't before.

questions.prompt: What do you remember most from school?

options.label: My friends

insight.reveal: People who remember friends first often measure any place by its people. The same people tend to choose jobs and homes partly by who's around.
insight.step: This week, send a short message to someone from your school days.

options.label: A subject I loved

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests a love of learning that started early. People like this often still have a trace of that subject in their adult hobbies.
insight.step: Spend ten minutes this week on that old subject, just for fun.

options.label: A teacher who believed in me

insight.reveal: People who remember one believing teacher often know how much a single voice can change a path. They tend to become that voice for someone else later.
insight.step: This week, tell someone you believe they can do something they're unsure about.

options.label: A moment I felt stupid

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people who hold one old moment as proof of something. The child in that moment didn't have the tools you have now.
insight.step: Think of that moment and say what you know now that the younger you didn't.

questions.prompt: When you read a book, you usually…

options.label: Read it start to end

insight.reveal: People who read straight through often like to give things a fair chance. The same patience tends to show up with people they don't like at first.
insight.step: Next book you don't enjoy, give yourself permission to stop at chapter three.

options.label: Read several books at once

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you match the book to the mood. People like this often handle many projects at work too, and feel bored with only one thing on the plate.
insight.step: This week, notice which book you reach for when tired, and which when curious.

options.label: Peek at the ending first

insight.reveal: People who read the ending first often enjoy the journey more when they know where it goes. The same need for certainty can show up in travel plans and talks with a boss.
insight.step: Next time you feel the urge to peek, wait one more chapter and notice the feeling.

options.label: Rarely finish, but remember one line forever

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who read for sparks, not stories. One great line can do more for them than a finished book.
insight.step: This week, write down one line you love from anything you read.

questions.prompt: In a class or talk, you don't understand something. You…

options.label: Ask right away

insight.reveal: People who ask right away often help the whole room, because others were lost too. They tend to learn faster, and quietly make others braver.
insight.step: Next time, notice if anyone thanks you after you ask a question.

options.label: Ask after it's over

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you like one-to-one learning. People like this often get deeper answers, because a private question gets a real reply.
insight.step: Next time, ask your question after, then share the answer with one other person.

options.label: Look it up later myself

insight.reveal: People who search alone often prefer not to depend on others to learn. It builds strong skills, and sometimes makes asking for help at work feel harder than it should.
insight.step: This week, ask one question you'd normally look up yourself.

options.label: Nod and hope it makes sense later

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people who'd rather be lost than look lost. The pattern can show up in conversations too: nodding through things to keep the moment smooth.
insight.step: Next time you nod without understanding, ask one small question: 'Can you give an example?'

questions.prompt: Being a total beginner at something feels…

options.label: Exciting

insight.reveal: People who love being a beginner often treat mistakes as part of the fun. The same attitude tends to make them easy to teach and fun to learn with.
insight.step: This week, try one thing you've never done, even something small like a new recipe.

options.label: Uncomfortable, but I get through it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you can hold discomfort without running from it. People like this often surprise themselves by how much they learn after the first awkward week.
insight.step: Next time you feel clumsy learning something, say 'day one' to yourself.

options.label: Embarrassing, so I practise alone first

insight.reveal: People who practise alone first often want to arrive already good. It works, but it can make learning slower and lonelier than it needs to be.
insight.step: Show one person something you're still learning this week, before it's good.

options.label: So bad I quit before anyone sees

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who were praised for being 'naturally good' at things. Being bad at something then feels like losing who you are. It's a story worth questioning.
insight.step: Pick one thing you quit and try it again privately for ten minutes.

questions.prompt: Someone asks you to explain something you know well. You…

options.label: Love it and go into detail

insight.reveal: People who love explaining often learn things a second time while teaching them. They tend to remember what they've taught better than what they've only read.
insight.step: This week, explain one thing you know to someone who asked, then ask them what stuck.

options.label: Keep it short and simple

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you respect people's time and attention. People like this are often great at instructions and dislike long meetings.
insight.step: Next time you explain something, ask 'Want more detail?' at the end.

options.label: Get impatient when they don't get it fast

insight.reveal: People who feel impatient often forgot how hard it was to learn. The same speed that makes them experts can make them hard to learn from.
insight.step: Next time, explain it using one example from the other person's life.

options.label: Suddenly doubt I really know it

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people who know a lot but trust themselves little. Friends may judge your ability more accurately than you do.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.
insight.step: Ask a friend this week what they think you're good at explaining.

questions.prompt: You get feedback with one compliment and one criticism. What stays with you?

options.label: The compliment

insight.reveal: People who remember the compliment often bounce back fast. The twist: they sometimes miss the useful part of criticism, so it's worth a second look.
insight.step: Next feedback you get, write down one thing from the criticism to try.

options.label: Both, equally

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you hear feedback as information, not a verdict. People like this often grow fast because they don't need to defend themselves first.
insight.step: This week, give someone balanced feedback the way you'd like to receive it.

options.label: The criticism

insight.reveal: People who remember criticism often care deeply about doing well. The criticism usually feels louder than it was meant to be, and the compliment was just as true.
insight.step: Next time, read the compliment twice before you read the criticism.

options.label: The criticism, and I start rewriting myself

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who take feedback about one task as feedback about the whole self. Feedback is usually about the work, not you.
insight.step: Next feedback, finish this sentence: 'This is about my work on ___, not about me.'

questions.prompt: The last new thing you learned was mostly for…

options.label: Work or school

insight.reveal: People who learn mostly for work often enjoy feeling useful. The hidden pattern: they may rarely give themselves time to learn just for joy.
insight.step: This week, learn one small thing that's only for fun.

options.label: Fun

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests curiosity drives you more than reward. People like this often carry a strange collection of facts and skills that surprise others.
insight.step: Share your newest fun skill or fact with someone this week.

options.label: Keeping up with others

insight.reveal: People who learn to keep up often feel a quiet race around them. The race is often less crowded than it looks, since others feel the same way.
insight.step: Pick one thing to learn this month that nobody around you cares about.

options.label: Proving someone wrong, maybe me

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people who use doubt as fuel. It works, but learning tends to feel lighter once the proving is over.
insight.step: Next time you learn something, notice the moment it stops being about proof.

questions.prompt: A friend cancels your plans an hour before. What's your first feeling?

options.label: Honestly? Relief

insight.reveal: People who feel relief often love the friend and their own quiet evening at the same time. The cost was usually the plan, not the person, which is why relief and fondness can sit side by side.
insight.step: Next time you make plans, suggest something low-effort, like a short walk, and notice if you look forward to it more.

options.label: No problem, we'll find another day

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who see friendship as a long game. The hidden catch: easy-going friends often end up being the one who always does the rescheduling.
insight.step: This week, when a plan moves, let the other person pick the new day instead of you.

options.label: Annoyed, I was already getting ready

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you start investing in a plan early, in your head and your outfit. People like this are often let down less by the missed evening than by the sense that effort wasn't matched.
insight.step: Next time someone cancels, tell them kindly in one sentence that you were looking forward to it.

options.label: I wonder if they're avoiding me

insight.reveal: People who choose this often read a cancellation as a message about themselves. The same quick alarm tends to show up when a reply is slow or a tone feels flat, even though the real reason is usually boring.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time a plan falls through, think of three dull reasons it could have happened before deciding what it means.

questions.prompt: You realise a good friend's birthday was yesterday. What do you do?

options.label: Send a warm late message

insight.reveal: People who pick this trust that warmth matters more than timing. Friendships like yours often run on steady small signals instead of big gestures, and those quiet signals tend to be what lasts.
insight.step: Pick one friend whose birthday you don't know and find it out this week.

options.label: Plan something to make up for it

insight.reveal: This answer tends to belong to people who show love by doing. The twist: part of that energy may be about calming your own guilt, which is why the plan can grow bigger than the friend expected.
insight.step: Next time you feel you owe someone, try a small gesture first and see if it is enough.

options.label: Admit I forgot and say sorry

insight.reveal: Choosing honesty over a smooth cover story suggests you'd rather be known than look perfect. People like this often become the friend others trust with their own small failures.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: This week, admit one small slip to someone before they notice it themselves.

options.label: Act as if I meant to message today

insight.reveal: People who choose this often care so much about not letting others down that they hide the slip. The same instinct can appear at work, where small mistakes get fixed quietly before anyone sees.
insight.step: Next time you forget something small, try saying "I forgot, sorry" and notice how little actually changes.

questions.prompt: You post in the group chat and nobody replies for hours. What do you do?

options.label: Nothing, chats move fast

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests silence doesn't carry much meaning for you. People like this tend to give others the benefit of the doubt in other places too, like a short email from a boss.
insight.step: This week, notice one moment when someone else reads too much into silence, and gently offer them a boring explanation.

options.label: Reread what I wrote

insight.reveal: People who reread often have a quiet editor in their head who keeps working after the message is sent. That same editor usually makes them thoughtful writers, and tired ones.
insight.step: Next time you want to reread a sent message, wait ten minutes first and see if the urge passes.

options.label: Send a joke to cover it, or delete it

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who feel exposed when a message hangs there unanswered. Humour becomes a way to take the risk back. The friends who matter rarely notice the gap at all.
insight.step: Next time, leave the unanswered message alone for a day and see what actually happens.

options.label: Mute the chat and pull back for a while

insight.reveal: People who choose this often protect themselves by leaving first. The hidden pattern: stepping back feels safe, but it can make the next silence feel even louder.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: This week, reply to one message in a group chat you've been quietly avoiding.

questions.prompt: Your closest friend moves far away. What happens to the friendship?

options.label: We set up regular calls

insight.reveal: People who pick this protect friendship with structure, the same way others protect a gym habit. Your choice suggests you know that good intentions alone rarely survive a busy month.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Put one call with a faraway friend in your calendar for a specific day this week.

options.label: We drift, but pick up easily when we meet

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people whose friendships are deep enough to survive silence. The risk is quiet: years can pass between "we should talk" moments without anyone deciding it.
insight.step: Send a faraway friend a photo of something that reminded you of them today.

options.label: I wait for them to reach out

insight.reveal: People who choose this often worry about being a bother, so they wait to be invited. The twist: your friend may be waiting for exactly the same reason.
insight.step: This week, reach out first to one friend you've been waiting on. One line is enough.

options.label: I quietly grieve it, almost like a breakup

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you take friendship as seriously as romance, which many people never admit. That depth is not a weakness: strong friendships are among the most protective things in life.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: Tell one friend, in plain words, how much their friendship has meant to you.

questions.prompt: A friend proudly shows you something they made, and it isn't good. What do you say?

options.label: Something kind and general

insight.reveal: People who pick this protect the moment over the work. You may be the friend people show things to first, and that early trust is easy to lose if you ever switch to blunt.
insight.step: Next time someone shows you their work, name one specific detail you liked instead of a general compliment.

options.label: I praise the best part and skip the rest

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who are honest by choosing what to say, not by saying everything. The same skill often makes them good at calming arguments without lying.
insight.step: This week, when giving feedback, try praising one part and asking one curious question about another.

options.label: I ask what kind of feedback they want

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you see feedback as a request, not a duty. People like this often get honesty back in return, because others feel safe asking them hard things.
insight.step: Next time someone shares something they made, ask: do you want cheering or ideas?

options.label: The truth, as gently as I can

insight.reveal: People who choose this tend to believe that kindness without truth doesn't last. Interestingly, friends often see our strengths more clearly than we see our own, so your honest eye may be valued more than you think.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.
insight.step: This week, ask a trusted friend for one honest piece of feedback on something of yours.

questions.prompt: In your friendships, who usually reaches out first?

options.label: It's pretty even
