insight.reveal: People who pick this often have friendships that feel easy because nobody is quietly counting. That balance usually comes from years of small, unnoticed effort on both sides.
insight.step: This week, thank a friend for always being there, without a reason or occasion.

options.label: Mostly me

insight.reveal: This answer tends to belong to the quiet glue of a friend group. The surprise: many friends of the person who always reaches out assume that person simply enjoys it and never wonder if they get tired.
insight.step: This week, skip being first once and see who reaches out to you.

options.label: Mostly them

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you enjoy friendship but rarely feel the pull to start it. People like this are often surprised to learn that their friends see their silence as distance, not calm.
insight.step: Message one friend first today, even just to say you thought of them.

options.label: Sometimes I stop, to see if they'll notice

insight.reveal: People who choose this are often quietly asking a question: "Do I matter here?" Tests like this feel safer than asking directly, but they rarely give a clear answer.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time you want to test a friend, try telling them you miss hearing from them instead.

questions.prompt: When did you last make a genuinely new friend?

options.label: Within the last year

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you still treat friendship as something that can grow, not just something you have. People like this often keep trying new places and hobbies well into later life.
insight.step: Invite someone you've only met a few times to do something simple this week.

options.label: A few years ago

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people whose lives got full: work, family, routines. New friends rarely appear on their own after school ends; they usually come from repeated, unplanned contact.
insight.step: Pick one place you visit weekly and say hello to the same person there next time.

options.label: I honestly can't remember

insight.reveal: People who choose this often have a few old friends and feel that's enough. Yet friendship is not a small extra: strong social ties are linked to a longer life, as strongly as many health habits.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: This week, reply to one message from an acquaintance with a question that keeps the talk going.

options.label: I've stopped trying, it feels awkward

insight.reveal: Your answer suggests the awkwardness feels bigger than the reward right now. People who feel this way often find that a fixed plan, decided in advance, removes most of the awkward part.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Make one when-then plan: "When I see a familiar face this week, I will ask them one question."

questions.prompt: A friend gets the exact thing you've been hoping for. Your honest first reaction?

options.label: Pure happiness for them

insight.reveal: People who pick this often keep their own hopes and their friends' wins in separate boxes. That skill tends to make them the first person others call with good news.
insight.step: Next time a friend shares good news, ask them two questions about it before saying anything about yourself.

options.label: Happy, with a small sting

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you can hold two feelings at once and admit it, which is rarer than it sounds. The sting usually points to exactly what you want next.
insight.step: Name the sting to yourself as a goal, then write one small step toward it this week.

options.label: I start comparing my life to theirs

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who measure themselves against those closest to them, not strangers. The same habit often shows up with siblings and coworkers too.
insight.step: Next time you catch yourself comparing, list one thing you have that you once hoped for.

options.label: I go a bit quiet with them for a while

insight.reveal: People who choose this often need time to sort out their feelings before facing the friend. The quiet is usually self-protection, but the friend may read it as you not caring.
insight.step: This week, send one short, sincere congratulations, even if the feeling isn't fully settled yet.

questions.prompt: A friend tells you a secret. Who ends up knowing?

options.label: Nobody, ever

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests people can feel when something is safe with you, often before you've proven it. Those who keep secrets well tend to be told more of them, which can be a quiet weight.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Check in with yourself this week: is there a secret you're carrying that you need help holding?

options.label: Maybe my partner, no one else

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who see a partner as part of themselves. Your friend may not see it that way, and that small gap is where many friend-partner tensions start.
insight.step: Next time you're told something private, ask: "Is it okay if my partner knows?"

options.label: It has slipped out once or twice

insight.reveal: People who admit this are often warm, talkative and close to many people at once. Secrets slip most often when we want to feel connected to the person we're talking with.
insight.step: Next time you feel a secret on your tongue, share a story about yourself instead.

options.label: I forget which things were secrets

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you live in the present and don't file information carefully. The same loose filing system often helps you forgive quickly, because you forget details of old hurts too.
insight.step: When a friend shares something private, repeat back "just between us" so it sticks in memory.

questions.prompt: A friend says something that hurts you. What do you usually do?

options.label: Laugh it off

insight.reveal: People who pick this often value the mood of the room over their own sting. It keeps things light, but the remark can return at 2 a.m. because it never got said out loud.
insight.step: Next time a comment stings, try a light but honest line: "Ouch, that one landed."

options.label: Mention it later, when I'm calm

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you separate the feeling from the conversation. People like this are often the ones friends trust in conflict, because they rarely strike in the moment.
insight.step: This week, raise one small thing you've been saving, using a calm "I felt…" sentence.

options.label: Talk it over with someone else first

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who think out loud. Careful, though: going over and over the person who hurt you tends to grow anger, not release it.
insight.research: People who vented anger while dwelling on the person who annoyed them became angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing.
insight.step: Next time you vent, set a short limit, then switch to talking about what you want to happen next.

options.label: Say nothing, but trust them a little less

insight.reveal: People who choose this often keep a quiet ledger instead of starting a hard conversation. The friend doesn't know the score is changing, which can make the distance feel mysterious to them.
insight.step: Pick one friend you've quietly pulled back from and tell them one thing that bothered you.

questions.prompt: Your phone shows a parent or older relative calling. What do you do?

options.label: Answer right away

insight.reveal: People who pick this often feel that family calls are never really optional. The same reflex tends to make them reliable at work, and sometimes reachable a bit too easily.
insight.step: This week, call an older relative first, before they call you.

options.label: Let it ring, call back later

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you protect your moment while keeping the bond. People like this often want family time on their own terms, not less of it.
insight.step: Pick a fixed time each week for family calls so they stop interrupting and start feeling planned.

options.label: Take a deep breath before picking up

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who switch into an older version of themselves the moment family calls. The breath is a small wall between who you are now and who you were at home.
insight.step: Before the next family call, decide one topic you'd enjoy talking about and bring it up early.

options.label: Send a message instead of calling back

insight.reveal: People who choose this often like contact they can control. A message lets you share news without the questions, the tone and the long goodbye that a call brings.
insight.step: This week, try one short call with a time limit you set yourself at the start.

questions.prompt: A long family visit is coming up. How do you get ready?

options.label: I just look forward to it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests family is a place you recharge, not drain. People like this often bring the calm others in the family depend on, without knowing they're doing it.
insight.step: During the visit, ask an older relative one question about their life at your age.

options.label: I plan a few breaks for myself

insight.reveal: People who pick this know their limits and plan around them, a sign of self-knowledge many people lack. The breaks often make the time together kinder, not shorter.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Decide in advance: "When I feel tense, I'll go for a ten-minute walk."

options.label: I rehearse answers to the usual questions

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who've been asked the same question for years: work, partner, plans. Rehearsing helps, but it can also make the visit feel like a test you must pass.
insight.step: Prepare one question to ask them instead, so you lead the talk for a while.

options.label: I find a reason to make it shorter

insight.reveal: People who choose this often love their family most from a short distance. Shorter visits aren't a failure. For some families, less time means kinder time.
insight.step: Plan one moment in the visit you'd genuinely enjoy, like a meal or walk, and protect it.

questions.prompt: Growing up, which role did you have in your family?

options.label: No clear role that I remember

insight.reveal: People who pick this often grew up with room to change from year to year. That freedom can show up later as an ease with new jobs and new groups.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.
insight.step: Ask a family member what role they think you had. Their answer may surprise you.

options.label: The peacemaker

insight.reveal: This answer tends to belong to people who still notice tension in a room before anyone speaks. That early radar is useful at work, but it can make your own needs come last.
insight.step: Next time there's tension nearby, wait a moment before fixing it and see if others step in.

options.label: The responsible one

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you learned early that things go better when you handle them. People like this often find it hard to rest while anything is still undone, even as adults.
insight.step: This week, hand one task you would normally do to someone else and let it be done their way.

options.label: The one who stayed out of the way

insight.reveal: People who choose this often grew very good at reading a room quietly. The same skill can make them sharp observers as adults, and slow to ask for space in a group.
insight.step: In your next group conversation, share one opinion early instead of waiting to be asked.

questions.prompt: Your family expects a life choice from you that you don't want. What do you do?

options.label: My family doesn't really push

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you grew up with room to choose. People like this are sometimes surprised by how much pressure their friends carry, and how hard it is for them to explain it.
insight.step: Ask a friend this week what their family expected of them. Then just listen.

options.label: I explain my choice and live with it

insight.reveal: People who pick this tend to accept that being understood may take years. The same steady patience often shows up when they defend a decision at work.
insight.step: Write down one sentence that explains your choice kindly, so it's ready next time it comes up.

options.label: I mostly go along with it

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who put family harmony above personal wishes. That loyalty is real love, but it's worth knowing which choices are truly yours.
insight.step: Pick one small choice this week, like a meal or plan, and make it purely for yourself.

options.label: I keep parts of my life private from them

insight.reveal: People who choose this often live two quiet versions of themselves. It protects peace, but the private part may be exactly what would help your family know you.
insight.step: Share one small, safe true thing about your life with a family member this week.

questions.prompt: A parent gives you advice you didn't ask for. What do you feel?

options.label: Grateful, mostly

insight.reveal: People who pick this often see advice as love in a clumsy form. That generous reading tends to make family time easier, and makes you easy to give advice to.
insight.step: Thank a parent or older relative for one piece of advice that actually helped you.

options.label: I nod and do it my way

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who stopped arguing because nodding is faster. It keeps peace, though the parent may never learn who you've become.
insight.step: Next time, share one reason you'll do it differently, calmly and briefly.

options.label: Suddenly fifteen years old again

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests a parent's voice can switch you back into an old version of yourself in seconds. Many capable adults feel this. It's a sign of an old pattern, not of who you are now.
insight.step: Next time it happens, notice your body first: shoulders, jaw. Relax one before you answer.

options.label: I argue, then hear their voice later anyway

insight.reveal: People who choose this often push back loudly because the advice landed. Weeks later the words return in your own head, sometimes as your own idea.
insight.step: Next time advice annoys you, ask yourself: what part of this might be true?

questions.prompt: A relative asks to borrow money. What's your first thought?

options.label: If I can, yes

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you see family resources as shared. People like this often give easily, and rarely ask for help back, even when they need it.
insight.step: This week, ask a family member for a small favour you would normally handle alone.

options.label: Yes, with a clear date to pay back

insight.reveal: People who pick this protect the relationship by making the money clear. The same clarity tends to show up in shared bills and group trips, and it saves friendships.
insight.step: Next time you lend anything, say the return date out loud at the start.

options.label: I'd rather give a smaller amount as a gift

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who've learned that loans can sour love. Giving, not lending, also feels better: spending on others tends to lift happiness more than spending on yourself.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: This week, buy a small treat for someone with no occasion and notice how it feels.

options.label: Dread, because of last time

insight.reveal: People who choose this often carry an old unpaid debt, financial or emotional. The dread is less about this request than about the earlier one that was never talked about.
insight.step: Decide your answer before the next request comes, so you don't have to decide in the moment.

questions.prompt: When do you notice that you're like one of your parents?

options.label: When I use one of their phrases

insight.reveal: People who pick this often find the resemblance funny rather than scary. Words are usually the first thing we inherit, and often the gentlest.
insight.step: Notice one phrase you got from family this week and tell them you still use it.

options.label: I don't think I'm like them at all

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you've worked to be different. But others often see us more clearly than we see ourselves, so a friend might spot a likeness you don't.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.
insight.step: Ask a close friend: "In what way am I like my parents?"

options.label: When I worry the way they worried

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who learned worry by watching it. The good news: patterns learned by watching can be changed by practising a different one.
insight.step: Next time a familiar worry starts, say out loud: "That's an old habit," and take one calm action.

options.label: When I lose my temper the same way

insight.reveal: People who choose this are often the ones most determined to stop a family pattern. Noticing it is the first and hardest step, and many never get that far.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Choose a plan: "When I feel my temper rise, I will step away for two minutes."

questions.prompt: An argument starts at a family meal. What do you do?

options.label: Change the subject

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you quietly manage the mood of the table. People like this often became the family's smoother early on, and many still do it at work.
insight.step: Next time, let a small disagreement run for a minute before stepping in.

options.label: Join in, I have opinions

insight.reveal: People who pick this often see arguing as a form of closeness. In some families, debate is love. Others at the table may not have learned that rule.
insight.step: At the next meal, ask someone quiet what they think before you share your view.

options.label: Find a reason to leave the room

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who learned that leaving is the fastest way to calm. You may also be the one who knows exactly when to bring dessert.
insight.step: Next time you step away, come back with one kind sentence for the person who seemed most upset.

options.label: Stay quiet, then replay it for days

insight.reveal: People who choose this often hold the whole argument inside, including the lines they didn't say. Replaying feels like solving, but it usually just keeps the anger warm.
insight.research: People who vented anger while dwelling on the person who annoyed them became angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing.
insight.step: Next time you replay an argument, write the one thing you wish you'd said, then put it away.

questions.prompt: When did you last tell a family member you love them, in words?

options.label: This week

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests love is said out loud where you come from, or where you've chosen to go. People like this tend to make it easier for others to say it back.
insight.step: Tell someone you love them in a new way this week: in a note, a voice message, or a look.

options.label: We show it, we don't say it

insight.reveal: People who pick this often speak love in food, fixing things and showing up. It's real, but younger family members sometimes need the words too.
insight.step: Next time you do something kind for family, add one sentence that says why.

options.label: I honestly can't remember

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who assume family already knows. Often they do, but hearing it can still change a day, and people are rarely sorry they said it.
insight.step: Pick one family member and say it before the week ends, even if it feels strange.

options.label: I want to, but the words get stuck

insight.reveal: People who choose this usually feel it deeply. The words get stuck because they matter. A fixed plan can take the pressure off the moment.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Make a plan: "When I end my next call with them, I'll say it."

questions.prompt: A family member needs help. Who usually steps up?

options.label: We share it fairly

insight.reveal: People who pick this are lucky, and often helped make it that way. Fair sharing in families usually comes from someone talking about it early, before resentment builds.
insight.step: Thank a sibling or relative this week for the part they carry.

options.label: Someone else, they live closer

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests distance shapes your role. People in this position often help in other ways, and sometimes feel guilt they never say aloud.
insight.step: Offer one specific thing you can do from afar, like a call or handling a task online.

options.label: Me, almost always

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who were the family's helper long before it was official. The same pattern often shows up in friend groups and teams at work.
insight.step: Ask one other family member for one specific piece of help this week.

options.label: Me, and I quietly resent it

insight.reveal: People who choose this often keep giving because stopping feels worse than resenting. Resentment is usually a signal that a need was never spoken, not that you love them less.
insight.step: Tell one family member one thing you need, in a single calm sentence.

questions.prompt: You and your partner disagree about something. What do you usually do first?

options.label: Talk it through right away

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests unsolved problems feel heavier to you than awkward talks. People like this often cool down by talking, which can surprise partners who cool down alone.
insight.step: Next time, ask your partner: "Now, or in an hour?" and let them choose.

options.label: Take time to cool off first

insight.reveal: People who pick this know their first words aren't their best ones. The key is coming back: the pause works best when your partner knows when it will end.
insight.step: Next time you need space, say when you'll come back to it, like "after dinner".

options.label: Make a sharp or sarcastic comment

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people with quick minds and quick hurt. Small mocking remarks can feel harmless, but in couples research contempt is one of the most damaging habits.
insight.research: In long-running studies of couples, contempt (mockery, eye-rolling) was the strongest single predictor of divorce.
insight.step: Next time a sharp line is ready, try saying the feeling behind it instead: "I'm hurt."

options.label: Go quiet until it passes

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel that silence keeps things from getting worse. Partners, though, often read silence as punishment, even when it's really self-protection.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time you go quiet, say one sentence first: "I need some time, I'm not leaving."

questions.prompt: With a partner, how do you handle money, or how would you?

options.label: Everything shared

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you see a couple as one team in practice, not just in words. People like this often find money talks easier, because there's nothing to divide.
insight.step: This week, choose one shared goal with your partner, small or big, and give it a name.

options.label: Some shared, some separate

insight.reveal: People who pick this like togetherness with a little private room. The same balance often shows up in how they share time, friends and even the sofa.
insight.step: Talk with your partner about one thing each of you would like to buy freely, no questions asked.

options.label: Fully separate

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who value independence and fairness highly. Separate money can work well, but talk about big future plans early, before they surprise you.
insight.step: Have one short talk this week about a shared goal for the next year.

options.label: Separate, and some spending stays private

insight.reveal: People who choose this often want to avoid judgment more than hide something big. Small secrets about spending tend to grow more from fear of a reaction than from the spending itself.
insight.step: Share one small purchase with your partner that you'd normally keep to yourself, and see how it lands.

questions.prompt: At home, who notices that something needs doing?

options.label: We both notice

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you share the invisible work too, the planning and remembering, not just the doing. Couples who share this tend to argue less about chores.
insight.step: Thank your partner this week for one task you know they always remember.

options.label: Mostly me

insight.reveal: People who pick this often carry a running list in their head all day. The tiring part is usually not the chores but being the only one who remembers them.
insight.step: Hand over one whole task, including remembering it, to your partner this week.

options.label: Honestly, mostly my partner

insight.reveal: This answer takes honesty, and that suggests fairness matters to you even when it isn't flattering. Partners who notice less often never learned to look, not that they don't care.
insight.step: This week, take one task you never think about and own it completely.

options.label: Me, and I keep a quiet list of who did what

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel unseen more than overworked. A secret score usually grows larger than the chores themselves, because the other person doesn't know it exists.
insight.step: Instead of keeping score, ask for one specific thing this week, out loud.

questions.prompt: Your partner's phone is unlocked next to you. What happens?

options.label: Nothing, I don't look

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests trust feels natural to you, not like effort. People like this often extend the same easy trust to friends and coworkers, and expect it back.
insight.step: This week, tell your partner one thing you trust them with completely.

options.label: I glance if a message pops up

insight.reveal: People who pick this are often simply curious, the same way they read a stranger's book cover on a train. It's usually about attention, not doubt.
insight.step: Next time you're curious, just ask: "Who was that?" Simple questions keep things light.

options.label: Tempted, even though I trust them

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people whose trust is real but whose worry has its own voice. The two can live together. Worry usually speaks louder when you're tired or stressed.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time the urge comes, notice what kind of day you've had before acting on it.

options.label: I have looked before

insight.reveal: People who choose this often look for calm, not for proof. The relief rarely lasts, because the feeling came from inside, not from the phone.
insight.step: Next time you want to check, tell your partner one worry instead, in a calm sentence.

questions.prompt: After a fight, who usually says sorry first?

options.label: Whoever was more wrong

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you see apologies as fair, not as weakness. Couples who work this way tend to get over fights faster because nobody is protecting pride.
insight.step: Next time, apologise for your part even if it was the smaller part.

options.label: Me, to end the tension

insight.reveal: People who pick this often can't relax while things feel wrong between you. The risk: sorry becomes a tool for peace instead of a real conversation.
insight.step: Next time you apologise, add one sentence about what you actually need.

options.label: Usually my partner

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who find apologies harder to say than to feel. Your partner may be doing quiet work that deserves a thank-you.
insight.step: This week, be the first to say sorry for one small thing.

options.label: Nobody, we just move on

insight.reveal: People who choose this often prefer forgetting to repairing. It keeps life calm, but unspoken fights can return later in surprising forms, like a sharp joke.
insight.step: After the next disagreement, ask one gentle question: "Are we okay?"

questions.prompt: At a party, your partner laughs a lot with someone new. You feel…

options.label: Glad they're having fun

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests your partner's joy doesn't feel like your loss. People like this tend to give partners room, and partners often come back closer because of it.
insight.step: Tell your partner later what you liked about seeing them happy.

options.label: Curious who that is

insight.reveal: People who pick this tend to turn small worries into questions instead of stories. That habit protects relationships more than most people realise.
insight.step: Next time, join the conversation and ask the new person a real question.

options.label: A small knot in my stomach

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who feel closeness in their body. The knot isn't a fact about your partner; it's often an old alarm that rings early.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time you feel the knot, breathe out slowly and look for one sign that you're still connected.

options.label: Cooler toward them later, without saying why

insight.reveal: People who choose this often hope the partner will notice and ask. They usually don't, and the evening ends confused on both sides.
insight.step: Next time, say one honest sentence: "I felt a bit left out tonight."

questions.prompt: You get a whole evening at home without your partner. You feel…

options.label: Freedom, finally

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you love your partner and also need yourself. People like this often come back to the relationship warmer after time alone.
insight.step: Plan one evening alone this month and use it for something you truly enjoy.

options.label: I miss them quite quickly

insight.reveal: People who pick this tend to feel home as a person rather than a place. The same pull often shows up when travelling or when friends move away.
insight.step: Next time you're alone, try one small activity you'd never do with them around.

options.label: A bit lost, unsure what to do

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who've shaped much of their life around the couple. It's worth knowing which interests are yours alone.
insight.step: This week, start one small thing that is just yours: a book, a walk, a recipe.

options.label: Relief, then guilt for feeling relieved

insight.reveal: People who choose this often believe that loving someone means always wanting them near. Needing space is not a sign of weak love; it's usually a sign of a full life.
insight.step: Tell your partner, kindly, that you enjoy a little time alone, and ask if they do too.

questions.prompt: When did you last thank your partner for something ordinary?

options.label: Today

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you notice the small work of daily life. Partners who feel noticed for ordinary things tend to keep doing them, without being asked.
insight.step: Thank your partner for one thing tomorrow that you've never thanked them for before.

options.label: Sometime this week

insight.reveal: People who pick this often feel thankful more often than they say it. The feeling is there; the habit just hasn't caught up.
insight.research: In one study, new daily habits took a median of 66 days to become automatic, and missing a single day did not ruin progress.
insight.step: Link thanks to a daily moment: when you sit down to eat, name one thing they did.

options.label: I'm not sure

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people in long relationships, where effort becomes background. Ordinary thanks is small, but its absence is felt.
insight.step: This week, thank your partner for one boring, regular task.

options.label: I'd thank them more if they thanked me

insight.reveal: People who choose this are often waiting for proof they're seen. Couples sometimes wait on each other in silence. One person going first can change the whole pattern.
insight.step: Go first once this week: thank them, then notice if anything shifts.

questions.prompt: A big shared decision, like moving home. How do you decide?

options.label: Long talks until we agree

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you see a shared decision as a shared process, not a vote. People like this often take longer but rarely regret the path they chose together.
insight.step: For your next shared choice, each write your top three wishes, then compare.

options.label: I research and lead, they approve

insight.reveal: People who pick this tend to feel calmer with a plan in their hands. Be curious, though: your partner may have quiet wishes they never voice because the plan is already so complete.
insight.step: Next time, ask your partner what they hope for before you start researching.

options.label: I mostly go with what they want

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who value peace and trust their partner's judgment. Over time, though, a life built on someone else's choices can start to feel borrowed.
insight.step: Share one strong preference this week, even on something small like a meal.

options.label: I decide in my head, then persuade

insight.reveal: People who choose this often think fast and privately. The decision may be right, but partners can feel brought in late. That feeling lasts longer than the decision.
insight.step: Next time, share your thinking while it's still half-formed.

questions.prompt: After a terrible day, what do you need most from your partner?

options.label: An hour of space

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you need to settle before you can share. People like this often seem cold right after a hard day, though they're really just recharging.
insight.step: Tell your partner your recharge time in advance, so they know it isn't about them.

options.label: Just listen, no advice

insight.reveal: People who pick this often solve things best out loud. Advice, even good advice, can feel like a sign you weren't heard.
insight.step: Start the next talk with: "I just need you to listen for a bit."

options.label: Help me fix it

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who feel calmer when there's a next step. Partners who just listen may seem caring to others, but to you it can feel like being left alone with it.
insight.step: Next time, ask your partner: "Can you help me think of one step?"

options.label: For them to notice without me saying

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel truly loved when they're read without words. It's a lovely wish, but even close partners guess wrong, and we often assume others see what we see.
insight.research: People tend to overestimate how many others share their own choices and opinions (the false consensus effect).
insight.step: Next hard day, say one plain sentence: "Today was rough, I need a hug."

questions.prompt: You enjoyed a first date. When do you message them?

options.label: The same night

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you'd rather show interest than play it cool. People like this tend to find out quickly where they stand, which saves months of guessing.
insight.step: Next time you enjoy someone's company, friend or date, tell them that day.

options.label: The next day

insight.reveal: People who pick this often like a small pause to check their feelings. It's a quiet sign of someone who trusts the second feeling more than the first.
insight.step: Next time you feel unsure about someone, wait one night, then decide.

options.label: I wait for them to message first

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who want to be chosen before they choose. The same pattern can appear with friends and jobs: you wait to be sure you're wanted.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time you like someone, send the first message within a day.

options.label: I rewrite the message many times first

insight.reveal: People who choose this often care so much that the words become the test. The other person usually reads a message in seconds and remembers only the warmth.
insight.step: Next time, write the message once, wait a minute, then send it.

questions.prompt: You get to plan a first date. What do you choose?

options.label: Coffee, easy to leave

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you like an exit door. People who pick this often protect their time and others' feelings in the same move.
insight.step: Next time you meet someone new, suggest a short plan and let it grow if it's going well.

options.label: An activity, like a walk or class

insight.reveal: People who pick this tend to relax when there's something to do side by side. The same people often have their best talks in cars and on walks, not across tables.
insight.step: Take one conversation you've been putting off and have it while walking.

options.label: A proper dinner

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who treat dating as worth real effort. It's also a quiet test: you learn a lot about someone from how they treat a long meal.
insight.step: Notice this week how people you meet treat staff or strangers; it says a lot.

options.label: Whatever they suggest

insight.reveal: People who choose this often want the other person comfortable more than they want their own preference met. It's kind, but it can leave them knowing you less.
insight.step: Next time someone asks what you'd like, name one real preference.

questions.prompt: Do you ever look at an ex's social media?

options.label: Never

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests once something ends, you close the door fully. People like this often move on quickly, though some later find old feelings arrive all at once.
insight.step: Think of one good thing a past relationship taught you, and let it be just that.

options.label: Now and then, out of curiosity

insight.reveal: People who pick this often see exes like old chapters they reread. Curiosity isn't longing; it's usually about checking how far you've come.
insight.step: Next time you look, notice how you feel after. Then decide if it's worth it.

options.label: Mostly after a bad day

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who use the past as comfort when the present hurts. The ex is rarely the point; the day is.
insight.step: Next bad day, message a friend before you open any profile.

options.label: More often than I'd admit

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel the story ended before they were ready. Checking keeps the story open a little. Worry about rejection can shape how long that takes to close.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Mute or hide one account this week, just for seven days, and see how it feels.

questions.prompt: Early on, what makes you lose interest the fastest?

options.label: They're rude to a waiter

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you judge character by how people treat those with less power. People who pick this tend to value honesty and humility above charm.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: This week, notice someone who is kind to strangers and tell them you noticed.

options.label: They stay on their phone

insight.reveal: People who pick this tend to value full attention as the clearest sign of interest. You probably give it too, and notice quickly when it isn't returned.
insight.step: Next time you're with someone you care about, put your phone in a bag for the whole meal.

options.label: They seem too keen, too soon

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who need closeness to grow slowly. Strong early interest can feel like pressure, even when it's simply warmth.
insight.step: Next time someone is very warm early, give it one more date before deciding.

options.label: They like me more than I like myself

insight.reveal: People who choose this often trust interest more when it's harder to win. Being liked easily can feel strange when your inner voice is harsher than theirs.
insight.step: Write down one thing a past partner or friend loved about you, and read it twice.

questions.prompt: Think of your past crushes. Do they have something in common?

options.label: Not really

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests attraction for you follows the person, not a pattern. People like this are often surprised by who they fall for, and enjoy it.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.
insight.step: Ask a close friend if they see a pattern you don't. Friends often notice more than we do.

options.label: A similar look

insight.reveal: People who pick this know what catches their eye first. The more revealing part is often what makes them stay, which may be very different.
insight.step: Think of the person you stayed interested in longest and name one quality that wasn't about looks.

options.label: They were a little out of reach

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who feel most alive in the chase. Calm, available people can feel boring at first, and sometimes they turn out to be the deepest.
insight.step: Next time someone kind and available shows interest, give it a second chance.

options.label: They remind me of someone in my family

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel pulled toward what feels like home, whether home was calm or chaotic. Noticing the pattern gives you a choice the pull doesn't.
insight.step: Name one family trait you'd love a partner to have, and one you'd rather not repeat.

questions.prompt: Someone you like is replying more slowly than usual. What do you do?

options.label: Assume they're busy

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you don't build stories from small gaps. People like this tend to be easy company, because they don't need constant proof.
insight.step: Next time a friend worries about a slow reply, share your calm reading with them.

options.label: Check when they were last online

insight.reveal: People who pick this often turn small data into big meaning. The check feels like it will calm you, but it usually adds a new question instead.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time you want to check, set your phone face down for twenty minutes first.

options.label: Slow my replies to match

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who protect themselves by keeping things even. It feels fair, but it can turn two interested people into two careful strangers.
insight.step: Next time, reply at your natural pace and see what happens.

options.label: Quietly start losing interest

insight.reveal: People who choose this often switch off before they can be hurt. It's fast protection, but it can end things that just needed one honest question.
insight.step: Next time you feel interest fading, ask once: "Still keen to meet?"

questions.prompt: Someone great wants to make it official. What do you feel first?

options.label: Happy, let's do it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests commitment feels like a door opening, not closing. People like this tend to bring that same easy yes to new jobs, cities and friendships.
insight.step: Tell the people close to you something you're happy about this week.

options.label: Nervous, in a good way

insight.reveal: People who pick this tend to feel big moments fully. The nerves usually mean it matters, not that something is wrong.
insight.step: Next time you're nervous about something good, name it out loud as excitement.

options.label: A little trapped

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who value freedom deeply. The trapped feeling is often about losing yourself, not about the other person.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Name one thing you'd keep for yourself in any relationship, and say it early.

options.label: Doubt they really mean it

insight.reveal: People who choose this often wait for the catch, even with good news. That doubt usually comes from older stories, not from what this person has done.
insight.step: Next time someone says something kind, reply only with "thank you" and nothing else.

questions.prompt: The bill arrives on a first date. What do you do?

options.label: Offer to split

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests fairness matters to you from the start. People like this tend to dislike feeling owed or owing, in love and in friendship.
insight.step: Notice this week where you feel you owe someone, and let one small debt go.

options.label: Pay, I invited them

insight.reveal: People who pick this often show care through generosity. Giving to others tends to lift our own mood, which may be part of why it feels so natural.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: Treat someone this week to something small, with no reason.

options.label: Let them pay if they offer

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who are comfortable receiving, a rarer skill than giving. Letting others be generous can be a kindness too.
insight.step: Next time someone offers you something, just say thank you instead of refusing first.

options.label: Freeze and wait to see what they do

insight.reveal: People who choose this often read social rules carefully and fear getting them wrong. The other person is very likely feeling the same small panic.
insight.step: Before your next shared meal, decide what you'll offer, so the moment is easy.

questions.prompt: On early dates, how much of the real you shows up?

options.label: All of it, take it or leave it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you'd rather be rejected for who you are than liked for a version. People like this tend to find fewer matches but much better ones.
insight.step: This week, share one honest opinion in a setting where you'd usually stay neutral.

options.label: A polished version

insight.reveal: People who pick this tend to treat first impressions like a job interview. It works, though the real you may be more interesting than the polished one.
insight.step: On your next new meeting, share one small odd thing you love.

options.label: It comes out over weeks

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who open slowly but fully. Others may underestimate them early, then be surprised how much is there.
insight.step: Tell someone new one personal story earlier than you normally would.

options.label: There's one part I hide until I'm sure

insight.reveal: People who choose this often carry one part of themselves they fear is too much. That part is usually less unusual to others than it feels from inside.
insight.step: Share a small piece of that hidden part with a trusted friend this week.

questions.prompt: After a few dates, you're not feeling it. How do you end it?

options.label: A clear, kind message

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you see clarity as kindness. People like this tend to handle hard work conversations well too, because they don't hide in vague words.
insight.step: This week, say one clear no you've been putting off, kindly and briefly.

options.label: Tell them face to face

insight.reveal: People who pick this believe the other person deserves their presence for bad news too. It's brave, and it's often remembered with respect long after.
insight.step: Next time you must give hard news, think of one kind true sentence to start with.

options.label: Reply less and less until it fades

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who hate hurting others directly. The fade feels gentler, but it often leaves the other person guessing much longer.
insight.step: Next time, send one short honest line: "I enjoyed meeting you, but I don't feel a match."

options.label: Keep going a bit longer so they're not hurt

insight.reveal: People who choose this often carry other people's feelings as if they were their own. The same habit can keep you in jobs and plans long after you know.
insight.step: Notice one thing you're doing only to avoid disappointing someone, and plan a kind exit.

questions.prompt: A stranger on the street looks lost. What do you do?

options.label: Walk over and ask if they need help

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you act before the moment passes. People like this often break the spell that keeps a whole crowd waiting for someone else to move.
insight.step: This week, offer help to one stranger before they ask.

options.label: Help if they ask me

insight.reveal: People who pick this often worry about intruding. Most lost people are relieved, not offended, when someone offers first.
insight.step: Next time you see someone confused, make eye contact and smile. That alone invites them to ask.

options.label: Assume someone else will help

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people in busy places, where everyone thinks the same thing. Being honest about it is the first step to being the exception.
insight.step: Next time you think "someone else will", be that someone, once.

options.label: I want to help but feel too shy

insight.reveal: People who choose this usually notice others' trouble more than most. The care is already there; only the first sentence is missing.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Prepare one line in advance: "Can I help you find something?" Use it once this week.

questions.prompt: A neighbour you barely know asks you to water their plants for a week.

options.label: Say yes, happily

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests small favours feel like connection to you, not cost. People like this often become the neighbour everyone knows by name.
insight.step: Introduce yourself to one neighbour you haven't met yet.

options.label: Say yes, then worry I'll forget

insight.reveal: People who pick this take responsibility seriously, almost too seriously. The same worry often makes them very reliable, at a quiet cost to their calm.
insight.research: In one study, new daily habits took a median of 66 days to become automatic, and missing a single day did not ruin progress.
insight.step: Set one reminder linked to a daily habit, like after brushing your teeth.

options.label: Find a polite excuse

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who protect their time and privacy. That's fair, but small favours are often how strangers turn into a real community.
insight.step: Offer one tiny favour this week that fits your own schedule.

options.label: Say yes, then wish I'd said no

insight.reveal: People who choose this often find saying yes easier than the moment of saying no. The same pattern tends to fill their calendar with other people's priorities.
insight.step: Next request you get, say "Let me check and get back to you" before answering.

questions.prompt: Some unexpected extra money arrives. What would you enjoy most?

options.label: Saving it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests future comfort feels better to you than a quick treat. People like this often find it easy to wait, and harder to enjoy money once they have it.
insight.step: Spend a tiny part of the next surprise on something purely fun, and notice how it feels.

options.label: A treat for myself

insight.reveal: People who pick this tend to celebrate good luck right away. That joy is real; the twist is that things we buy often fade faster than memories we make.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: Next treat, choose an experience instead of an object and compare how long the happy feeling lasts.

options.label: A day out or trip

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who collect memories, not things. People often say experiences made them happier than possessions, and you seem to know that already.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: Plan one small experience this week, like a new walk or meal, with someone you like.

options.label: Quietly spending it on someone else

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel happiest when joy moves outward. The research agrees: money spent on others tends to lift our own happiness more than money spent on ourselves.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: This week, buy a small surprise for someone and don't tell anyone else.

questions.prompt: Where are you with volunteering?

options.label: I do it regularly

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests giving is part of your routine, not a mood. People like this often gain as much as they give: new friends, purpose and a reason to leave home.
insight.step: Invite one friend to join you next time you volunteer.

options.label: Now and then, when someone asks

insight.reveal: People who pick this tend to help through people, not causes. A friend's request matters more than a poster. That's why your help often goes where it's needed most.
insight.step: Ask one friend this week if they need help with anything.

options.label: I keep meaning to start

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people with good intentions and full weeks. The gap usually isn't caring; it's the missing first step.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Make a plan: "On Saturday morning, I will look up one place nearby that needs help."

options.label: I help in private, informal ways instead

insight.reveal: People who choose this often dislike attention for being kind. Their help is real, often hidden, and many people around them may not know how much they give.
insight.step: Continue one quiet kindness this week, and let it stay unseen.

questions.prompt: You helped someone a lot and nobody noticed. How do you feel?

options.label: Fine, that wasn't the point

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you help for the help itself. People high in honesty and humility tend to act the same whether or not anyone is watching.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Do one small helpful thing today that nobody will ever know was you.

options.label: I find a way to mention it

insight.reveal: People who pick this want their effort to be real to others. That's human; being seen is a basic need. Asking for recognition directly often feels better than hinting.
insight.step: Next time you feel unseen, say simply: "I worked hard on that, I'd love a thank-you."

options.label: A little hurt, honestly

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who give generously and quietly hope it's noticed. The hurt is a sign of how much you put in.
insight.step: Thank someone else this week for a quiet effort they made. Notice how it feels to give that.

options.label: I remember it for a long time

insight.reveal: People who choose this often keep a private record of unrewarded effort. Over time the record can weigh more than the help itself.
insight.step: Pick one old unnoticed effort and let it go, out loud: "I did that because I wanted to."

questions.prompt: You're struggling with something. How easily do you ask for help?

options.label: Easily

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you see help as a normal part of life. People like this often make others feel useful, and are helped more because of it.
insight.step: Ask someone for a small piece of advice this week, just to let them help.

options.label: Only for practical things

insight.reveal: People who pick this will ask for a lift but not for comfort. The line between those can be thin, and others often want to help with both.
insight.step: This week, tell one person how you're really feeling, not just what you need done.

options.label: Only when it's almost too late

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who believe their problems shouldn't trouble others. The same people are usually first to help when someone else struggles.
insight.step: Ask for help with one thing this week while it's still small.

options.label: I'd rather help someone else

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel safer giving care than receiving it. Being needed feels comfortable; needing feels exposed. Both directions build the bonds that protect us.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: Let someone do one small thing for you this week and simply say thank you.

questions.prompt: A coworker or classmate is clearly overwhelmed. What do you do?

options.label: Offer to take something off their plate

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you see help as action, not words. People like this often become the ones a team leans on, sometimes more than they realise.
insight.step: Next time you offer help, name one specific task instead of saying "let me know".

options.label: Bring them a coffee or snack

insight.reveal: People who pick this know that small comfort can matter as much as big help. It's a gentle way of saying "I see you" without adding pressure.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: Surprise someone who's busy with a small treat this week.

options.label: Wait until they ask

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who respect others' independence. The catch: overwhelmed people often don't ask, which is part of why they're overwhelmed.
insight.step: Next time someone looks stressed, ask one gentle question: "How are you holding up?"

options.label: Keep my head down, I have my own pile

insight.reveal: People who choose this are honest about their limits, which many aren't. Protecting your energy is not unkind. Even a short kind word costs little and lands well.
insight.step: Send one short supportive message to a busy coworker this week.

questions.prompt: You find a wallet on the ground. What happens next?

options.label: Hand it in where it can be claimed

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests doing right feels automatic to you. People like this tend to stay honest even when nobody would ever know.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Notice one small rule you follow even when no one is watching, and give yourself credit.

options.label: Look inside and contact the owner myself

insight.reveal: People who pick this want to finish the job personally. The same drive often makes them the one who follows up on lost emails and forgotten tasks at work.
insight.step: This week, finish one small task someone else started and forgot.

options.label: Leave it where it is, they may come back

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who think from the owner's side first. It's a thoughtful instinct, even if the wallet might wait a long time.
insight.step: Next time you see something lost, ask a nearby shop or staff member what to do.

options.label: Return it, then wonder if they'd do the same

insight.reveal: People who choose this act well but keep a quiet question about fairness. The question isn't cynical; it shows how much you hope others are good too.
insight.step: This week, notice one example of a stranger being kind and remember it.

questions.prompt: Which small kindness did you do most recently?

options.label: Held a door or let someone go first

insight.reveal: People who pick this keep small courtesies alive, the kind that make streets and shops feel human. Many never notice they do it every day.
insight.step: This week, add one word to the gesture: a smile and "after you".

options.label: Checked on someone who'd gone quiet

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you notice absence, not just presence. People like this often catch friends at exactly the moment they needed it, without knowing it.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: Check on one more person this week who has been quiet for a while.

options.label: Gave a stranger a real compliment

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who say the kind thought others keep inside. Strangers often remember a sincere compliment for years.
insight.step: Give one specific compliment to someone this week, about a choice they made, not their looks.

options.label: I can't think of one

insight.reveal: People who choose this often do small kindnesses so naturally they don't count them. Or life has been too full lately. Either way, noticing is the start.
insight.step: Do one small kind thing on purpose tomorrow, and notice it.

questions.prompt: Someone asks a favour you really don't have time for. You…

options.label: Say no, kindly

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you trust relationships to survive a no. People like this are often asked less, but when they say yes, it's fully meant.
insight.step: Next time you say no, add one thing you can do, even if it's small.

options.label: Offer a smaller version

insight.reveal: People who pick this look for the middle path. It keeps both your time and their trust, and often teaches others what's realistic to ask.
insight.step: Prepare a small offer in advance: "I can't do that, but I can do this."

options.label: Say yes and stretch myself

insight.reveal: This answer tends to come from people who measure their worth partly by how useful they are. The same stretch often shows up at work, where tired helpers are easy to miss.
insight.step: Next time you want to say yes automatically, pause for one breath and ask: do I have time?

options.label: Say yes, then do it late or half-heartedly

insight.reveal: People who choose this often say yes to avoid an awkward moment, then pay for it later. The other person usually would have preferred an honest no.
insight.step: Next time, say "Let me check" first, then answer within a day.

questions.prompt: Think of a really good day you had. What made it good?

options.label: Everything went to plan

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel joy as relief: a good day is one where nothing went wrong. The same pattern can make holidays oddly tiring, because surprises feel like work instead of fun.
insight.step: On one free day this week, leave one hour with no plan and notice how it feels.

options.label: I finally finished something hard

insight.reveal: People who pick this often treat happiness as a reward that must be earned first. A lovely day with nothing finished can leave them strangely restless, as if they skipped a step.
insight.step: One evening this week, note one good thing that happened that you did not have to earn.

options.label: A long talk with someone I like

insight.reveal: This answer tends to point to joy built in conversation, not in events. People like this often remember a trip less by the places and more by who said what at dinner.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: Before the week ends, invite one person for a talk with no other purpose: a walk, a call, a tea.

options.label: Hours alone where nobody needed me

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests your best days are defined by what is missing: requests, noise, other people's moods. People who pick this often give a lot all week and only feel the cost when the quiet arrives.
insight.step: Put a two-hour 'nobody needs me' block in your calendar this week and protect it like a meeting.

questions.prompt: Something small goes well for you. Who do you tell first?

options.label: Nobody, I just enjoy it quietly

insight.reveal: People who pick this often hold good news like a warm drink: privately and slowly. The hidden cost: others rarely learn what makes you happy, so they can't help create more of it.
insight.step: Next time something small goes well, tell one person within the hour and watch their face.

options.label: My partner or closest friend

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show one person is your 'joy witness'. Good news only feels finished once they have heard it, which says a lot about how much space that person holds in your life.
insight.step: This week, ask your closest person about their small win before you share yours.

options.label: The group chat, with a photo

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel happiness grow as it bounces off others. The replies are part of the joy, so a silent chat can make a good moment feel smaller than it really was.
insight.step: Next time you share good news, notice if the joy peaks before the replies arrive, or after.

options.label: Someone whose approval still matters to me

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests a win becomes real once a certain person sees it. Many people carry one 'approval audience' from long ago, and it quietly shapes which goals they choose at all.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: After your next small win, wait one minute and decide how proud you are before telling anyone.

questions.prompt: An unexpected free afternoon appears. What do you do with it?

options.label: Rest on the sofa, no guilt

insight.reveal: People who choose this often know how to switch off on purpose, a skill many adults lose. The twist: the 'no guilt' part is usually the rarer talent, not the resting itself.
insight.step: Next free hour, rest fully, then name one thing that made it feel restful.

options.label: Go somewhere I've never been

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show that newness is how you recharge, not something that drains you. People like this can often remember a single new street better than a whole month of routine weeks.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: This week, take a different route home or eat somewhere new, and notice what you remember a day later.

options.label: Catch up on tasks I've been avoiding

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests free time feels like a debt to repay first. People who pick this often enjoy rest more after one small task, but the list can grow to fill every gap if allowed.
insight.step: Next free afternoon, do exactly one task, then spend the rest on something you enjoy.

options.label: Scroll my phone and somehow lose it

insight.reveal: This honest answer often comes from tiredness, not laziness: when choosing feels like work, the phone chooses for you. The afternoons people remember tend to be decided in the first five minutes.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Make a when-then plan: 'When free time appears, I will pick one activity before I unlock my phone.'

questions.prompt: A friend shares big news online. What's your first honest feeling?

options.label: Pure happiness for them

insight.reveal: People who choose this often measure their life against their own past, not against friends. That habit protects their mood, and it makes them the friend people tell good news to first.
insight.step: This week, send one friend a message saying exactly why their news made you happy.

options.label: Happy, then I quietly check my own life

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show a fast, private scoring system running in the background. Very human. The revealing part is which area you check first: it often points to what you want most right now.
insight.step: Next time you compare, notice which part of your life you checked, and name it in one word.

options.label: A small sting I'd never admit out loud

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests envy works for you as a signal, not a flaw. A sting usually points straight at something you want but haven't let yourself go after yet. Noticing it is often the first move.
insight.step: Next time you feel that sting, ask: what exactly do I want here? Then pick one tiny step toward it.

options.label: I scroll past fast or mute them

insight.reveal: People who pick this often protect their mood by limiting what comes in, which can be wise. The twist: skipping a friend's news can feel like distance to them, even when the cause was only your hard week.
insight.step: If you scroll past someone's news this week, come back a day later and react when you feel ready.

questions.prompt: Someone does something kind for you. How do you respond?

options.label: A quick thank you, then move on

insight.reveal: People who choose this often keep kindness light and even, so no one feels in debt. The hidden pattern: they may also find it hard to ask for help, because asking breaks the same balance.
insight.step: This week, thank someone with one specific detail about what their kindness changed for you.

options.label: I feel I must return it soon

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you keep a quiet balance sheet of kindness. It makes you reliable, but a gift can feel like a task until it is repaid, which steals some of its warmth.
insight.step: Next time someone is kind, wait a full week before giving anything back, and just enjoy receiving.

options.label: I feel awkward, like I don't deserve it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests receiving is harder for you than giving. People like this are often generous partly because giving feels like the safer role. Letting kindness land is a skill that can be practised.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time someone is kind, say only 'Thank you, that means a lot' and stop. No 'you didn't have to'.

options.label: I wonder what they want from me

insight.reveal: People who pick this often learned somewhere that kindness comes with a price. That guard made sense back then. The interesting question is whether the people around you now have earned the same caution.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: This week, accept one small kindness without looking for the reason, and see what actually follows.

questions.prompt: You get some unexpected money. What would make you happiest?

options.label: Saving it

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel happiness as safety. The joy is not in the money but in the quiet it buys in their head, which is why a bigger cushion can feel better than a bigger treat.
insight.step: This week, picture what 'safe enough' looks like for you, so saving has a finish line.

options.label: A trip, a concert or a great meal

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you buy memories rather than objects. People like this often retell the story for years, and the retelling seems to be where much of the value lives.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: Plan one small experience this month, then tell someone the story afterwards.

options.label: Treating someone I love

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests your happiness travels through other people's faces. People who pick this often forget to treat themselves, and only notice after a generous month leaves them feeling oddly empty.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: This week, do one small kind thing for someone else, and one for yourself.

options.label: The thing I've wanted for months

insight.reveal: People who choose this often have a wish ready and waiting. A wish held for months is rarely an impulse. Often the planning and waiting give as much pleasure as owning it a month later.
insight.step: Before buying, picture using it on an ordinary weekday a month from now. Still exciting? Enjoy it.

questions.prompt: How do your mornings usually start?

options.label: Slowly, with something warm to drink

insight.reveal: People who choose this often protect a small ritual that sets their mood for hours. The twist: when the ritual gets skipped, the whole day can feel 'off' without them knowing why.
insight.research: In one study, new daily habits took a median of 66 days to become automatic, ranging from 18 to 254 days, and missing a single day did not ruin progress.
insight.step: On a rushed morning this week, keep just two minutes of your ritual and see if the day feels different.

options.label: Phone first, before my feet touch the floor

insight.reveal: This answer tends to mean your first feelings of the day belong to other people's news and requests. People who change only this one habit often say their mornings start to feel longer, not shorter.
insight.step: For three mornings, keep the phone out of reach until you've had water or daylight.

options.label: Rushing, already a bit behind

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests your mornings start in debt. People with this pattern often guard their late evenings fiercely, because night is the only time that feels truly theirs. That trade explains a lot.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Make one when-then plan: 'When my alarm rings, I will stand up and drink water.' Try it for three days.

options.label: With a heavy feeling about the day ahead

insight.reveal: People who pick this often feel the day's weight before anything has happened. Usually the heaviness is tied to one specific thing, and naming it tends to make the rest of the morning lighter.
insight.step: Tomorrow morning, name the one thing behind the heavy feeling, then do the smallest part of it first.

questions.prompt: Which of these has given you the most joy lately?

options.label: A really good meal

insight.reveal: People who choose this often find joy through the senses, one of the most dependable sources there is. They also tend to notice weather, smells and textures that others walk straight past.
insight.step: At one meal this week, eat the first three bites with no phone and full attention.

options.label: Helping someone with a problem

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show joy that comes from being useful. People like this can feel strangely lost on holidays, because nobody needs anything from them. Usefulness can be planned into rest too.
insight.step: This week, offer help with something small that nobody asked for, and notice your mood after.

options.label: Getting better at something

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you enjoy the climb more than the view. People who pick this often get bored soon after mastering something, then quietly start looking for the next hard thing.
insight.research: In one study, new daily habits took a median of 66 days to become automatic, ranging from 18 to 254 days, and missing a single day did not ruin progress.
insight.step: Pick one skill and practise it for ten minutes on three days this week. Missing a day is fine.

options.label: Honestly, it's hard to say right now

insight.reveal: This honest answer often shows up in busy or flat seasons, when duty has pushed joy aside. It is usually quiet, not gone. Small, specific pleasures tend to bring it back faster than big plans.
insight.step: Each evening this week, notice one moment that was even a little bit good, however small.

questions.prompt: You reach a goal you worked hard for. How do you celebrate?

options.label: Properly, with people around me

insight.reveal: People who choose this often make wins feel real by sharing them out loud. The same habit makes them good at celebrating others, which quietly builds the support they lean on later.
insight.step: This week, celebrate someone else's small win as loudly as you would your own.

options.label: A small private treat

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show a calm, steady relationship with success. People like this rarely crash after big moments, because they never put all their joy into one moment in the first place.
insight.step: Choose your next small treat now, before the goal, and tie it to a clear finish line.

options.label: I'm already thinking about the next goal

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests the finish line moves the moment you touch it. People who pick this often achieve a lot and remember little of it, because they never paused long enough to store the feeling.
insight.research: Personality traits predict life outcomes such as health, divorce and career success about as well as family income and intelligence do.
insight.step: Next time you finish something, wait one full day before starting a new goal.
