options.label: It feels oddly flat when I get there

insight.reveal: People who choose this often discover that the chase, not the prize, held the meaning. That is common after big goals, and it usually signals a need for a deeper reason next time, not a bigger target.
insight.step: Before your next goal, say in one sentence why it matters to you, not only what it is.

questions.prompt: It's the last day of a holiday. What's on your mind?

options.label: Grateful it happened

insight.reveal: People who choose this often close good chapters cleanly. That skill keeps happy memories bright, because they aren't mixed with the sadness of the ending.
insight.step: On the last day of your next break, tell someone your three best moments out loud.

options.label: Already planning the next one

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you run on looking forward. For people like this, the weeks of waiting can hold as much joy as the trip itself, so having something planned matters more than its size.
insight.step: This week, put one small thing to look forward to in your calendar, even just coffee with a friend.

options.label: Dreading normal life and messages

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests ordinary life feels like something to escape. People who pick this often find that one specific part of their week drains them, not all of it. Finding that part can matter more than any trip.
insight.step: This week, notice which single part of your normal week you dread most. Just name it to yourself.

options.label: Sad that I never really relaxed

insight.reveal: People who choose this often bring their to-do list on the trip. The body rests while the mind keeps checking. Many find the first days of a break are spent just learning to switch off.
insight.step: On your next day off, put your work apps out of sight for the whole day.

questions.prompt: After a bad day, what helps you first?

options.label: Food and a show

insight.reveal: People who choose this often know that comfort for the body comes before sense for the mind. The twist: they're usually ready to talk about the bad day the next morning, not that night.
insight.step: After your next bad day, take the comfort first, and give yourself until morning before thinking it over.

options.label: Telling someone the whole story

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you understand your own day by saying it out loud. People like this often find the answer halfway through the story, before the listener has said a word.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: Next bad day, ask someone to just listen for five minutes, no advice needed.

options.label: Walking or moving until it fades

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you work through feelings with your body before words. People who pick this often think more clearly in motion, and some of their best decisions are made mid-walk.
insight.step: On your next stressful day, take a ten-minute walk before replying to anything important.

options.label: Nothing really, I replay it in bed

insight.reveal: People who choose this often try to solve the day by reviewing it again and again. Replaying feels like working on it, but after the first time through it rarely adds anything new.
insight.step: Tonight, if the replay starts, write down the one thing you'd do differently, then close the notebook.

questions.prompt: When stress builds up, how do you usually notice it first?

options.label: My shoulders or jaw get tight

insight.reveal: People who choose this often hear stress from their body before their mind admits it. That's useful: the body can act as an early warning, sometimes days before the worried thoughts arrive.
insight.step: Three times this week, check your jaw and shoulders and let them drop for one slow breath.

options.label: I snap at people over small things

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show stress leaking out sideways, onto whoever is nearest. People who notice this are often surprised how rarely the snapping is about the person in front of them.
insight.step: Next time you snap, say 'Sorry, that's stress, not you' within the hour.

options.label: Someone else tells me I seem stressed

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you keep going until others see it before you do. People like this are often the calm one in a crisis, and the last to notice their own tank is empty.
insight.step: Ask one person you trust: 'What's the first sign you notice when I'm stressed?'

options.label: My sleep goes first

insight.reveal: People who pick this often find their mind saves its worrying for when the day finally goes quiet. Thoughts that feel huge in the middle of the night often look much smaller in daylight.
insight.step: Keep paper by your bed. If a worry wakes you, write it down so your mind can set it aside until morning.

questions.prompt: You don't get something you really hoped for. What happens next?

options.label: I shrug and move on quickly

insight.reveal: People who choose this often bounce back fast. The quiet trade-off: they sometimes move on before learning what the hope was really about, and then chase a very similar goal again.
insight.step: Next disappointment, give it five minutes and ask: what did I actually want from this?

options.label: I look for what I did wrong

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you prefer a lesson over a loss. It turns pain into something useful, but it can also make you take the blame for things that were mostly luck.
insight.step: Next time, name one part that was in your control and one part that was simply luck.

options.label: I tell myself not to hope so much next time

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests disappointment teaches you to want less. It protects you, but people who pick this often notice later that they quietly stopped going after things they truly wanted.
insight.step: This week, say out loud one thing you still hope for, even if it might not happen.

options.label: I feel low for days and keep it to myself

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel deeply and hurt quietly. Others may think you're fine, so you end up carrying it alone. Sharing even a small piece of it tends to shorten the low stretch.
insight.step: Next time you feel low for more than a day, tell one person one sentence about it.

questions.prompt: When do you feel most alone?

options.label: The last evening of the weekend

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel the gap between free time and the week ahead. The loneliness is often about missing structure more than missing people, so a small plan for that evening can help a lot.
insight.step: Next weekend, plan one small thing for its last evening: a call, a walk or a meal with someone.

options.label: In a crowd or at a party

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you need depth, not just people. A room full of short chats can feel lonelier than a quiet evening at home, and that isn't strange at all.
insight.step: At your next gathering, aim for one real conversation instead of many short ones.

options.label: When good news comes and there's no one to tell

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests loneliness hits you hardest in joy, not in sadness. Sharing is how happiness becomes complete for you, and the feeling points to exactly who you wish you could call.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: Next time you have good news, send it to one person you've drifted away from.

options.label: Sometimes even with my partner or family

insight.reveal: People who pick this often feel unseen by the people closest to them. It's more common than people admit, and it often means one important part of you hasn't been shared yet, not that the bond is weak.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: This week, tell someone close one thing you care about that they may not know.

questions.prompt: Your to-do list is far too long. What do you actually do?

options.label: Do the easy things first

insight.reveal: People who choose this often need momentum before courage. Small wins warm them up. The risk is a day full of ticks where the one thing that really mattered is still waiting.
insight.step: Tomorrow, do one easy task, then the hardest one before lunch.

options.label: Rewrite the list in a better order

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you calm stress by organising it. Planning feels like progress and sometimes is. People like this do best when the new list starts with a task done in the next ten minutes.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Next time you rewrite a list, add one when-then plan: 'When I finish lunch, I will start task one.'

options.label: Freeze and scroll instead

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests that when everything feels urgent, nothing can start. Freezing is usually overload, not laziness. People like this tend to move again once the list is cut down to just one thing.
insight.step: Next time you freeze, cover the list and do only the top line for ten minutes.

options.label: Work late until it's all done

insight.reveal: People who pick this often trust effort more than limits. It works for a while. The hidden pattern: the list tends to grow to fill the hours you give it, so late nights rarely make it shorter.
insight.step: Pick a stop time for one evening this week and keep it, even with tasks left.

questions.prompt: Something sad happens. What do you do with the feeling?

options.label: Keep busy so I don't think about it

insight.reveal: People who choose this often get through hard weeks by staying in motion. It works short term. The feeling tends to wait patiently and return in quiet moments, like on holiday or late at night.
insight.step: This week, give a sad feeling ten minutes on purpose, then go back to your day.

options.label: Music or a film that matches the mood

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you let feelings run their full course instead of fighting them. People like this often feel better sooner, because the feeling is allowed to finish.
insight.step: Make a short playlist for low days now, while you feel fine.

options.label: Let myself cry if it comes

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you see tears as a release, not a weakness. People who pick this often recover quietly and fully, and they're often the ones others feel safe crying in front of.
insight.step: Next time someone near you is sad, sit with them for a minute before saying anything.

options.label: Hide it so nobody worries

insight.reveal: People who choose this often protect others from their feelings. It's kind, but it means the people who love you rarely get the chance to care for you back, and many of them want that chance.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: This week, tell one trusted person 'I'm a bit sad today' and let them respond.

questions.prompt: It's the night before a hard day. How do you spend it?

options.label: Go to bed early

insight.reveal: People who choose this often treat their body as the main tool for tomorrow. Their quiet strength: they trust that a rested mind will handle what a worried mind could never fully plan.
insight.step: Before your next hard day, set an alarm for bedtime, not just for waking up.

options.label: Prepare everything, then prepare again

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show worry turned into action. Preparing helps up to a point; after that, people like this are mostly checking for comfort, not for missing pieces.
insight.step: Next time, prepare once, then put everything in your bag and agree with yourself not to reopen it.

options.label: Distract myself with something fun

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you sense that worrying the night before rarely changes the result. People like this often do well because they arrive fresh, not because they rehearsed.
insight.step: Choose a fun thing for the night before your next hard day, and plan it in advance.

options.label: Lie awake running through what could go wrong

insight.reveal: People who pick this often try to live tomorrow tonight, imagining every version of it. The mind is trying to protect you. The odd part: the real day is rarely like any version they rehearsed.
insight.step: Tonight, write the worst case and one thing you'd do if it happened. Then put the paper away.

questions.prompt: A friend asks 'How are you?' during a hard week. What do you say?

options.label: "Fine, thanks!"

insight.reveal: People who choose this often save real answers for the right moment and the right person. The cost is small but real: friends may not know when to show up for you.
insight.step: This week, answer 'How are you?' with one true detail, just once.

options.label: "A bit tired, but OK"

insight.reveal: This answer tends to be a half-open door: a hint that something is up, to see if the other person notices. People like this often feel closest to those who gently ask a second time.
insight.step: Next time you hint, add one more sentence even if they don't ask.

options.label: I make a joke about how bad it is

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests humour lets you share pain without making it heavy. It invites people in and keeps them at a safe distance at the same time. The right friend laughs, then asks what's really going on.
insight.step: After your next joke about a hard week, add one serious sentence.

options.label: The real answer, even if it's messy

insight.reveal: People who pick this often have fewer but deeper friendships. The truth can feel risky, but it gives others permission to be honest too, which is why people often open up to you first.
insight.step: This week, ask someone 'How are you, really?' and wait through the pause.

questions.prompt: Nobody has messaged you all day. What goes through your mind?

options.label: Nice, a quiet day

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel secure without constant proof of connection. Silence reads as peace, not as a message. That calm usually shows in relationships too: a late reply rarely worries them.
insight.step: Use your next quiet day to message someone you've been meaning to, just because.

options.label: I message someone first

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you start connection instead of waiting for it. People like this keep friendships alive that would otherwise fade, and sometimes wonder why they're always the one who writes.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: Notice this week who messages you first, and thank one of them for it.

options.label: I keep checking my phone

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests silence makes you wonder where you stand. People who pick this often read meaning into gaps that were really just busy days on the other side of the screen.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: On your next quiet day, leave your phone in another room for one hour and notice what you feel.

options.label: I wonder if people have forgotten me

insight.reveal: People who choose this often think about others far more than they believe others think about them. The gap is usually in visibility, not in care: people think of you more often than they message you.
insight.step: Ask one friend this week: 'Do you ever think of messaging someone and then forget?'

questions.prompt: On a tired, low evening, what are you most likely to reach for?

options.label: Something warm and a blanket

insight.reveal: People who choose this often comfort themselves the way they'd comfort a child: warmth, softness, quiet. It works because it tells the body it is safe before the mind agrees.
insight.step: This week, set up one corner of your home as your low-day spot, ready before you need it.

options.label: An old favourite show I've seen many times

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you rest best when nothing can surprise you. Knowing the ending is the point. People like this often choose familiar food and familiar places in hard weeks too.
insight.step: Next low evening, notice which old favourite you pick. It may point to a time you felt safe.

options.label: A call with someone who knows me well

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you recover by being known: no advice, just a voice that needs no background story. People like this usually have one or two such people, and those people rarely know it.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: This week, tell the person you'd call that they are your low-day person.

options.label: Online shopping I don't really need

insight.reveal: People who choose this often want a small promise that something good is coming. The joy is in waiting for the parcel more than in the thing, a need that planning something to look forward to can also meet.
insight.step: Next low evening, put items in the basket but wait until morning to decide.

questions.prompt: Someone cuts in front of you in a queue. What do you do?

options.label: Let it go, not worth it

insight.reveal: People who choose this often save their energy for battles that matter. The question worth asking: does it truly go, or does it come back as a story you tell later that evening?
insight.step: Next time you let something go, check an hour later: is it still on your mind?

options.label: Politely point out where the line starts

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you believe fairness should be said out loud, but calmly. People like this often become the one others quietly hope will speak up in meetings too.
insight.step: This week, practise one calm, short sentence for small unfair moments, like 'Sorry, the line starts here.'

options.label: Say nothing, but fume inside

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests your anger turns inward when it can't go out. People like this often look very calm, while inside they're writing a long speech they will never give.
insight.step: Next time you fume silently, breathe out slowly three times, then decide: say it or drop it.

options.label: Tell them clearly, even if it gets loud

insight.reveal: People who pick this often have a strong inner rule about fairness and little patience for watching it break. The same fire usually makes them fierce defenders of friends who are treated badly.
insight.step: Next time you confront someone, lower your voice on purpose and notice whether they listen more.

questions.prompt: On the road, another driver nearly hits you. What's your reaction?

options.label: A deep breath, then I forget it

insight.reveal: People who choose this often read others' mistakes as accidents, not attacks. That quick, generous guess about intent tends to make their whole day lighter, not only their journey.
insight.step: Next time someone cuts you off, imagine one innocent reason they might be rushing.

options.label: The horn, and maybe a gesture

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show a fast release that's over in seconds. People like this often get angry quickly and calm down quickly, and are surprised when others still remember the moment.
insight.step: On your next journey, notice how long the feeling lasts after you use the horn.

options.label: Shout at them where no one can hear

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests the car is a private room for feelings you don't show anywhere else. People who pick this are often very polite in public, and the road is where the day's pressure escapes.
insight.research: People who vented anger while dwelling on the person who annoyed them became angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing.
insight.step: Next time you want to shout, try one long out-breath instead and compare how you feel a minute later.

options.label: Still angry about it hours later

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel the danger again each time they replay it. The story keeps the anger alive long after the risk has passed, and it often spills onto whoever is home first.
insight.step: When you get home after a bad drive, tell the story once, then change the topic on purpose.

questions.prompt: In an argument with someone close, what do you tend to do?

options.label: Talk it through calmly

insight.reveal: People who choose this often believe problems shrink once they're named. The twist: a very calm person can accidentally make the other feel more upset, as if their feelings are too big.
insight.step: Next disagreement, say what you feel in one word before you explain your logic.

options.label: I need space before I can talk

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you think better alone than in the heat of it. It works best when you say when you'll come back, so the other person doesn't feel left out in the cold.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time you need space, say 'Give me twenty minutes, then let's talk' and come back on time.

options.label: I need to fix it right now

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests an unsolved argument feels unsafe to you. People who pick this often chase the other person to fix it fast, which can push someone who needs space even further away.
insight.step: Next argument, wait ten minutes before trying to fix it, and notice what the waiting feels like.

options.label: I get sarcastic or roll my eyes

insight.reveal: People who pick this often turn to sarcasm when they feel unheard. It feels sharp in the moment, but it tends to land as 'I look down on you', which is rarely what you actually meant.
insight.research: In long-running studies of couples, contempt (mockery, eye-rolling) was the strongest single predictor of divorce.
insight.step: Next time sarcasm rises, say the real complaint underneath it in plain words instead.

questions.prompt: Someone wronged you years ago. How do you feel about them now?

options.label: I barely think about it

insight.reveal: People who choose this often let go by losing interest, not by forgiving. The person simply stopped being important. It's a quiet kind of freedom that many people never reach.
insight.step: This week, notice one small annoyance you're still carrying and choose to drop just that one.

options.label: Forgiven, but I remember everything

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you separate the feeling from the lesson. People like this can be kind to someone again while never handing them the same key twice.
insight.step: Think of one person you've forgiven. Is there one small piece of trust you could safely give back?

options.label: It still stings when I think of it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests the hurt was never fully answered. Often what stings most is not the act itself, but that the other person never seemed to understand what it cost you.
insight.step: Write them a letter you'll never send. Say exactly what it cost you, then keep it or tear it up.

options.label: I'd still like them to admit it

insight.reveal: People who pick this often hold a strong sense of justice that waits for the record to be corrected. The hidden cost: your peace ends up waiting on someone who may never act.
insight.step: This week, ask yourself: what would I feel if they never admit it? Let the answer sit for a day.

questions.prompt: A colleague takes credit for your idea in a meeting. What do you do?

options.label: Nothing. It's not worth it

insight.reveal: People who choose this often value a calm team over personal credit. The pattern to watch: others may slowly learn that your ideas are free to take.
insight.step: Next time you share an idea, send a short written summary afterwards.

options.label: Add a detail only the real author would know

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show a clever, calm way of standing up for yourself. People like this rarely make scenes, but they usually make sure the truth finds its way back into the room.
insight.step: Before your next meeting, prepare one follow-up point about your own idea.

options.label: Talk to them privately afterwards

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you protect both your work and the relationship. People who pick this give others a chance to put things right, and they remember clearly who took that chance.
insight.step: If it happens again, start the private talk with 'I noticed…' and describe only what happened.

options.label: Stay angry for days and avoid them

insight.reveal: People who choose this often swallow the anger in the moment and carry it for a week. The other person may never know, which means you pay the whole cost of something they did.
insight.step: Choose one sentence you could say to them, and decide this week whether to say it or let it go.

questions.prompt: At home, which small thing irritates you most?

options.label: Dishes left in the sink

insight.reveal: People who choose this often read small habits as messages: 'They don't notice what I do.' The dishes are rarely the real complaint. Being seen usually is.
insight.step: This week, thank someone at home for one small thing they do, and see whether the dish issue softens.

options.label: Noise when I want quiet

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show your mind needs quiet to recharge, the way a phone needs a charger. People like this get called 'grumpy' when they're really just overloaded.
insight.step: Agree on one quiet hour at home this week, and use it fully.

options.label: Being interrupted when I'm focused

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests deep focus is precious to you and slow to rebuild. The anger is really about the cost of restarting. People like this often do their best work in long, protected blocks.
insight.step: Next time you need focus, tell people at home: 'Give me 30 minutes, then I'm all yours.'

options.label: Feeling like I'm the only one who helps

insight.reveal: People who pick this often carry the invisible tasks: remembering, planning, noticing. The irritation is about a load nobody else can see, and it grows fastest when it stays unspoken.
insight.step: This week, name one invisible task you do and ask someone to take it over for a week.

questions.prompt: You read an online comment that makes you angry. What do you do?

options.label: Close it and move on

insight.reveal: People who choose this often know their attention is worth protecting. The same skill tends to help them walk away from pointless arguments in real life too.
insight.step: This week, notice one moment your mood dropped because of something on a screen.

options.label: Read all the replies

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you look for someone who agrees, to confirm you're not alone. It often makes the anger grow, because the replies are full of other angry people.
insight.research: People tend to overestimate how many others share their own choices and opinions (the false consensus effect).
insight.step: Next time, read only the first three replies, then close the app.

options.label: Write a reply, then delete it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests the anger needs words, but not an audience. People like this often get the relief of saying it without paying the cost of a public fight.
insight.step: Next time, write the reply, wait an hour, then decide whether it's still worth sending.

options.label: Reply, then keep checking who answered

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel a duty to correct wrong ideas. The checking back is the part that keeps the anger going, sometimes for a whole evening.
insight.research: People who vented anger while dwelling on the person who annoyed them became angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing.
insight.step: If you reply to something this week, turn off notifications for that post straight after.

questions.prompt: Someone is 30 minutes late to meet you, with no message. How do you feel?

options.label: Fine, I find something to do

insight.reveal: People who choose this often carry a little bag of time-fillers: a book, a podcast, a walk. Their patience is partly planning, which turns waiting into free time.
insight.step: Keep one small time-filler with you this week and notice how waiting feels.

options.label: Annoyed. It's rude

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you treat time as a form of respect. People like this are usually early themselves, and quietly keep track of who isn't.
insight.step: Next time someone is late, tell them kindly how it felt instead of staying quiet.

options.label: Worried something happened to them

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests your mind jumps to danger before rudeness. People who pick this often feel relief and anger at once when the person arrives, and the anger comes out louder.
insight.step: Next time you wait, send one message asking if they're OK, then set a time to stop worrying.

options.label: Wondering if I matter to them

insight.reveal: People who pick this often read lateness as a sign of their place in someone's life. Usually it's about the other person's messy day, not about you, but the feeling can be very loud.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time, think of two other reasons they might be late before deciding what it means.

questions.prompt: You're blamed for something you didn't do. What's your first move?

options.label: Explain the facts calmly

insight.reveal: People who choose this often trust that the truth wins if it's laid out clearly. Their calm is powerful, but sometimes the other person needs to hear that you're hurt, not only that you're right.
insight.step: Next time, add one sentence about how it felt, not just what happened.

options.label: Gather proof before I say anything

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you don't trust words alone to protect you. People like this often keep old messages and notes, having learned early to rely on evidence.
insight.step: This week, try clearing up one small misunderstanding quickly, with words alone and no proof.

options.label: Take the blame to keep the peace

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests peace matters more to you than being right. People who pick this are easy to work with, but over time others may start to see them through mistakes they never made.
insight.step: Next time, try: 'That wasn't me, but I can help fix it.' Both parts are true.

options.label: Get angry and defend myself hard

insight.reveal: People who choose this often have a sharp sense of fairness that wakes up fast. Being wrongly blamed can feel like an attack on who you are, not just on what you did.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Make a when-then plan: 'When I feel blamed, I will take one breath and say one fact first.'

questions.prompt: After you lose your temper, what usually happens next?

options.label: I apologise quickly

insight.reveal: People who choose this often can't rest while a relationship feels off balance. A fast apology repairs a lot, though it can skip the part where the other person says how it felt.
insight.step: Next time you apologise, add 'How did that feel for you?' and really listen.

options.label: I act normal and hope it's forgotten

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you repair with actions instead of words: a cup of tea, a small favour. Some people read this perfectly; others are still waiting to hear the words.
insight.step: Next time, pair your kind action with one short spoken sentence: 'Sorry about earlier.'

options.label: I feel bad about it for a long time

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you judge yourself more harshly than the other person does. People like this often feel guilty long after the other person has forgotten the moment.
insight.step: Next time, ask the person directly: 'Are we OK?' Then believe the answer.

options.label: I explain why I was right to be angry

insight.reveal: People who pick this often need their reasons understood before they can soften. The anger usually had a fair point inside it; the trick is sharing the point without the heat.
insight.step: Next time, start with what you regret, and explain your reasons after that.

questions.prompt: A friend gives you a gift you don't like. What do you say?

options.label: "I love it!"

insight.reveal: People who choose this often see small lies as gifts too: a way to protect a nice moment. The same people are often trusted with secrets, because they put feelings first.
insight.step: Next time, find one thing about the gift you can honestly praise, and say that.

options.label: Thank them for the thought, not the gift

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you search for a sentence that is both kind and true. People like this often have a talent for diplomacy that shows up at work as well.
insight.step: This week, give one compliment that is completely true and very specific.

options.label: Hint later at what I'd really like

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you prefer fixing the future to correcting the past. People who pick this often deliver honesty in small, careful doses over time rather than all at once.
insight.step: Tell one close person this week about something you'd truly enjoy receiving.

options.label: Tell them gently it's not really me

insight.reveal: People who pick this often believe close friends deserve the truth, even about small things. It can sting at first, but friends of people like this tend to trust their praise more.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Before your next honest moment, plan a kind first sentence.

questions.prompt: You promised to help a friend, but now you'd rather stay home. What do you do?

options.label: I go anyway

insight.reveal: People who choose this often treat their word like a contract with themselves. The twist: they're also careful about promising in the first place, which can make them seem slow to say yes.
insight.step: This week, before agreeing to something, say 'Let me check and confirm tomorrow.'

options.label: Go, but feel quietly grumpy

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show your sense of duty is stronger than your mood. Your friend may still sense the grumpiness, which can cancel out some of the kindness you gave.
insight.step: Next time you go anyway, pick one thing to enjoy on the way there.

options.label: Tell them honestly I'm too tired

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you'd rather be honest about your limits than show up empty. People who pick this often have friendships where 'no' is safe, which makes their 'yes' mean more.
insight.step: Next time you cancel, offer one specific other time, so it feels like a change of plan, not a no.

options.label: Make up a reason I can't come

insight.reveal: People who choose this often worry that 'I don't feel like it' isn't a good enough reason. An invented excuse feels kinder, but it slowly teaches you that your real needs require a cover story.
insight.step: Next time, try a short true reason: 'I'm out of energy today. Can we move it?'

questions.prompt: You make a mistake at work that no one has noticed yet. What do you do?

options.label: Fix it and tell my team

insight.reveal: People who choose this often see mistakes as information, not judgement. Teams with someone like this tend to raise problems sooner, because one person made it feel safe.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: This week, mention one small mistake you made and what you learned, in a casual moment.

options.label: Fix it quietly, no need to say

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you care about results more than confessions. It's efficient. The risk: when a bigger mistake comes, nobody will have seen how well you handle them.
insight.step: Next small fix, mention it in one line: 'Found and fixed an error in this.'

options.label: Wait and see if anyone notices

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests the fear of looking bad is louder than the mistake itself. People who pick this often spend more energy worrying than the fix would ever have cost.
insight.step: Next time, set yourself a short deadline: if it isn't fixed by then, tell someone.

options.label: Hope it looks like a system problem

insight.reveal: People who choose this often work in places where mistakes are punished, not discussed. The habit usually comes from the room more than the person, so it's worth asking if your room is really like that.
insight.step: This week, watch how your manager reacts to someone else's mistake. It shows how safe honesty is there.

questions.prompt: A shop gives you too much change by mistake. What do you do?

options.label: Give it back right away

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel uneasy holding anything that isn't theirs. The same feeling tends to show up with time and credit too: they dislike taking more than their share.
insight.step: This week, notice one moment you got a little more than was fair, and decide what to do about it.

options.label: Small shop, I return it. Big company, maybe not

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show your honesty is about people, not rules: you protect whoever would lose out. People like this find rules easier to bend when no single person seems to get hurt.
insight.step: Next time you think 'it's a big company', picture the cashier who has to balance the till.

options.label: I'd notice later and not go back

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests your honesty is strong in the moment but weaker once effort is needed. Many people work this way: being honest is easy, going back to be honest is the harder part.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Make a when-then plan: 'When I notice an error later, I will fix it the next time I pass by.'

options.label: Keep it. Their mistake, not mine

insight.reveal: People who pick this often see the world as fair trades: mistakes cut both ways. Something curious: whatever we choose here, we tend to assume most other people would choose the same.
insight.research: People tend to overestimate how many others share their own choices and opinions (the false consensus effect).
insight.step: Next time luck goes your way, ask: would I want this back if I were the cashier?

questions.prompt: A friend tells you a secret. Who might you tell?

options.label: Nobody, ever

insight.reveal: People who choose this often become the keeper of many secrets. The quiet cost: they rarely share their own, because they know exactly how much weight a secret carries.
insight.step: This week, share one small personal thing with someone you know keeps secrets well.

options.label: Only my partner

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you see your partner as part of you, not as a third person. Your friends might see it differently, which is worth checking once.
insight.step: Next time someone shares a secret, ask: 'Is it OK if my partner knows?'

options.label: Maybe one person, if it's not too serious

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you sort secrets into heavy and light. The catch: the person who told you may have sorted it differently, and people rarely say which kind it was.
insight.step: Next time you hear a secret, simply ask: 'Is this just for me?'

options.label: It sometimes slips out without meaning to

insight.reveal: People who pick this often share because closeness feels like trading stories, so a secret becomes a gift for the next person. Simply noticing that pattern is usually enough to slow it down.
insight.step: When a secret is on the tip of your tongue this week, switch to a story about yourself instead.

questions.prompt: Splitting a group bill when you ordered much less. What do you do?

options.label: Split it evenly, no fuss

insight.reveal: People who choose this often value the evening over the maths. They usually accept small losses for smooth friendships, and quietly notice who always orders the most.
insight.step: Next group meal, notice how you feel when the bill arrives. That feeling is useful information.

options.label: Pay for exactly what I had

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show a strong sense that fairness should be exact. People like this are often trusted with group money, and sometimes judged as tight when they're really just precise.
insight.step: Next time, suggest your way kindly before the bill comes, not after.

options.label: Split evenly, but feel annoyed

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you put the group's comfort above your own, then pay twice: once with money, once with irritation. The money is often the smaller cost.
insight.step: Next time, try one light sentence: 'I'll just pay for mine tonight, if that's OK.'

options.label: Order more so it feels fair

insight.reveal: People who pick this often have a sharp eye for balance and a creative way to restore it. It shows how strongly fairness pulls on you, even when the fix costs you more.
insight.step: Next group meal, try paying only for your share and see if anyone even notices.

questions.prompt: When is it hardest for you to tell the truth?

options.label: In small talk, like 'How was your day?'

insight.reveal: People who choose this often save honesty for moments that matter. Small talk feels like a social script, not a real question, so a short answer doesn't count as a lie to them.
insight.step: Once this week, answer 'How was your day?' with one real detail.

options.label: When it would hurt someone I love

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you rank kindness above accuracy. People like this are often careful listeners, and they may hear far more truth than they ever say.
insight.step: Next hard truth, start with 'I'm telling you because I care' and see how it lands.

options.label: When it makes me look bad

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you know exactly where your honesty bends, which is rare. Most people notice this in others long before they notice it in themselves.
insight.step: This week, admit one small thing that makes you look a little less perfect, and watch the reaction.

options.label: When I'm being honest with myself

insight.reveal: People who choose this often find the most uncomfortable truths are the private ones. Noticing that is already the first step. Honesty with yourself tends to grow quietly, one small admission at a time.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.
insight.step: Ask one trusted friend: 'What's one thing about me you think I don't see?'

questions.prompt: You realise you were wrong in an argument you 'won'. What do you do?

options.label: Go back and say I was wrong

insight.reveal: People who choose this often care more about what's true than about winning. Being willing to lose is rare, and it makes others more open to changing their own minds around you.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: This week, say 'I was wrong about that' about one small thing, out loud.

options.label: Mention it casually much later

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you admit things best once the heat is gone. People like this usually get there, just slowly, and the other person may have stopped waiting by then.
insight.step: Next time you realise you were wrong, say so within one day.

options.label: Let it stand. The moment has passed

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you see arguments as closed events, not open files. The other person may still carry the old version, though, and it may shape what they believe about you.
insight.step: Think of one old argument you won but shouldn't have. Is there a light way to mention it?

options.label: Look for a new reason I was still right

insight.reveal: People who pick this often feel being wrong as a small loss of self, not just of a point. Most minds work this way. Catching yourself searching for new reasons is already the hard part.
insight.step: Next time you hunt for new reasons, ask: 'If they had said this, would I accept it?'

questions.prompt: When you post about your life online, how true is the picture?

options.label: I rarely post at all

insight.reveal: People who choose this often keep their real life and their shared life separate. It protects privacy, and it also means friends may miss the good things happening to you.
insight.step: This week, share one small good moment directly with one friend, not online.

options.label: True, but only the best bits

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you edit, like most people do. The interesting part: we compare our behind-the-scenes to everyone else's best bits, and forget we're doing the same editing.
insight.step: Next time you compare yourself to a post, remember one thing you chose not to post.

options.label: I share the hard parts too

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you'd rather be known than admired. People who pick this often get quiet 'me too' messages, and become a safe place for others without ever planning to.
insight.step: This week, reply kindly to someone who shared something hard online.

options.label: A bit better than real life, honestly

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel the pull of an audience, even a small one. The gap between post and life can feel lonely, because the version people like isn't quite the real you.
insight.step: For one week, post nothing, or post one thing exactly as it is.

questions.prompt: A work rule seems pointless and no one would notice if you skipped it. What do you do?

options.label: Follow it anyway

insight.reveal: People who choose this often trust that rules carry reasons they can't see. They're dependable, and others tend to hand them the tasks where small details really matter.
insight.step: This week, ask the reason behind one rule you follow without knowing why.

options.label: Follow it, but ask to change it

insight.reveal: This answer tends to show you respect systems enough to improve them. People like this are often the ones who make workplaces better, slowly and without drama.
insight.step: Pick one pointless rule and suggest one clear improvement to the right person this week.

options.label: Depends on my mood that day

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests your rule-keeping is strongest on good days. Tiredness lowers the bar for nearly everyone. Knowing what your tired self tends to do is half the battle.
insight.step: This week, notice one choice you made differently because you were tired.

options.label: Skip it quietly

insight.reveal: People who pick this often judge rules by their purpose, not by who made them. It saves time, and it also means your own sense of 'pointless' becomes the rule, so it's worth checking now and then.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Before skipping a rule this week, ask one colleague why it exists.

questions.prompt: It's 3 a.m. and something has gone badly wrong. How many people could you call?

options.label: Lots. I have a wide circle

insight.reveal: People who choose this often spread support across many people, so no single friendship carries too much weight. The hidden cost: you may know a lot about others while few know the full story of you.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: This week, tell one friend something real about your life that you usually keep light.

options.label: Two or three, and that feels like plenty

insight.reveal: This answer tends to belong to people who invest deeply and prune quietly. The same habit often shows up in how you shop or work: fewer things, chosen with care, kept for a long time.
insight.step: Send one of those two or three people a message today that has no question or request in it.

options.label: One, and I'd still hesitate to wake them

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you count people as close but still fear being a burden to them. People who answer this way often help others at 3 a.m. without thinking twice, yet would never ask for the same.
insight.step: Ask that one person for a small favour this week and notice how they actually respond.

options.label: Honestly, I'd handle it alone

insight.reveal: People who choose this often learned early that relying on yourself is safer than waiting for others. That skill is real, but it can make closeness feel like a risk instead of a rest.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment avoidance, a discomfort with closeness, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time something small goes wrong, tell one person about it the same day instead of after it's fixed.

questions.prompt: You open your wardrobe. What do you mostly see?

options.label: A few pieces I love and wear all the time

insight.reveal: People who keep a small, loved wardrobe often make decisions fast in other areas too. You probably dislike menus with too many choices and secretly enjoy ordering the same dish again.
insight.step: Pick tomorrow's outfit tonight and notice whether your morning feels lighter.

options.label: Lots of choice, some never worn

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who buy a version of who they might become: the bold shirt, the formal coat. The unworn pieces are less about clothes and more about lives you are still trying on.
insight.step: Wear one never-worn item this week, just once, and see who you feel like in it.

options.label: Things I'm keeping for 'one day'

insight.reveal: People who keep 'one day' clothes often keep 'one day' plans too: the trip, the class, the call. Your choice suggests you protect future versions of yourself, sometimes at the cost of the current one.
insight.step: Choose one 'one day' item and either wear it this week or give it away by Sunday.

options.label: Things I bought to feel better on a bad day

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests your wardrobe is partly a diary of hard days. People who notice this are usually more honest with themselves than most, and that honesty is where the pattern starts to loosen.
insight.step: Next time a bad day pulls you toward a shop, wait one night first and see if the wish is still there.

questions.prompt: You get one free week to travel. Which trip do you choose?

options.label: One place, slowly, like I live there

insight.reveal: People who travel slowly often judge a place by its ordinary moments: a bakery, a bus ride, a neighbour's dog. The same instinct tends to show up in friendships, where you value routine over big events.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: This week, visit one place near home twice instead of trying somewhere new.

options.label: Five places. See as much as I can

insight.reveal: This answer often comes from people who fear missing the one great thing more than they fear being tired. You may collect moments the way others collect objects, and remember the rush more than the details.
insight.step: On your next outing, pick one moment and stay with it for five full minutes before moving on.

options.label: The trip that will look best when I share it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests part of the joy of a trip, for you, lives in how it is seen afterwards. People who admit this are often more aware than most of how much other eyes shape their choices.
insight.step: Take one outing this week where you take no photos at all, then notice what you remember.

options.label: Stay home and finally do nothing

insight.reveal: People who choose rest over adventure are often running on less fuel than they show. The wish for a blank week tends to signal that your normal weeks hold more than anyone around you knows.
insight.step: Block one evening this week with nothing planned, and protect it like a meeting.

questions.prompt: You arrive at a big buffet. What's your plan?

options.label: A little bit of everything

insight.reveal: People who sample everything often hate closing doors. The same pull tends to appear in careers and hobbies: you prefer keeping options open to betting it all on one.
insight.step: At your next meal out, order the first dish that catches your eye without reading the rest.

options.label: Find the best dish and go back for it

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you are a scout, then a loyalist. People who eat this way often do the same with friends, music and places: a short search, then deep, steady loyalty.
insight.step: Revisit one favourite thing this week, a song, a café or a person, on purpose.

options.label: Eat enough to make it worth the price

insight.reveal: People who choose this often keep a quiet scoreboard of fairness. It protects you from being cheated, but the same scoreboard can turn a good evening into a test you have to win.
insight.step: Next time you pay for something, judge it by how you felt after, not by how much you got.

options.label: Take more than I want, then feel bad

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests the fear of missing out speaks louder than your stomach. People who notice this pattern often find it in their calendar too: saying yes to everything, then wishing they hadn't.
insight.step: At your next meal, serve half of what you think you want and go back only if you're still hungry.

questions.prompt: You're offered one more project at work. What do you do?

options.label: Say yes. More is more

insight.reveal: People who say yes easily often get their energy from momentum, not rest. You may do your best work when slightly overloaded and feel strangely flat during quiet weeks.
insight.step: Before your next yes, take ten seconds to name what you will do less of to make room.

options.label: Say no to protect the work I already have

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you measure yourself by finished work, not busy days. People who guard their focus like this are often quietly admired, and sometimes quietly resented by those who can't say no.
insight.step: Write down the one task this week that deserves your best hours, and do it first one morning.

options.label: Say yes, even though I'm already stretched

insight.reveal: People who choose this often believe their value is in being reliable. The twist: they tend to protect everyone's deadlines except the ones they set for their own life.
insight.step: This week, move one small request to 'next week' and see if anything actually breaks.

options.label: Say yes because saying no scares me

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests a 'no' feels less like a boundary and more like a risk to how people see you. That fear often runs deeper at home than at work, and naming it is a rare kind of courage.
insight.step: Practise one small, kind no this week, like turning down a meeting you don't need.

questions.prompt: How do you usually read books, or watch series?

options.label: One at a time, start to finish

insight.reveal: People who finish one story before starting another often need closure in life too. An unanswered message or an unclear plan may bother you more than it bothers the people around you.
insight.step: Leave one small thing unfinished on purpose tonight and notice how long it nags at you.

options.label: Several at once, depending on my mood

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you use stories to manage your mood, picking the one that matches the day. People like this often have friends for different moods too, and rarely mix them.
insight.step: Notice which story you reach for on a hard day this week. It may tell you what you need.

options.label: I go back to the same favourites again

insight.reveal: People who rewatch and re-read often choose comfort because the rest of life asks for so many unknowns. A known ending is a small place where nothing can surprise you.
insight.step: Try one new thing this week that a person who knows you well recommended.

options.label: I start many and finish almost none

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you love beginnings, the moment when anything is possible. The same pattern often appears with plans and projects, where the exciting start fades before the slower middle.
insight.step: Pick one thing you started and finish just the next chapter or episode this week.

questions.prompt: How many photos are on your phone right now?

options.label: Not many. I delete as I go

insight.reveal: People who keep few photos often trust their memory more than their phone. You may also be quicker than most to let go of old arguments, objects and versions of yourself.
insight.step: Pick one photo you kept and send it to the person in it, with no message.

options.label: Thousands. I'll sort them one day

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who want to keep every door open, just in case. The 'one day' pile tends to grow in other places too: inboxes, tabs, and half-planned trips.
insight.step: Spend five minutes deleting photos from one single day. Stop when the timer ends.

options.label: Thousands, and I never look back at them

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests taking the photo is the point, not seeing it again. People like this often live forward and find the past less interesting than what comes next.
insight.step: Open a photo from exactly one year ago tonight and notice what you had forgotten.

options.label: I photograph moments instead of being in them

insight.reveal: People who notice this about themselves often feel a quiet worry that good moments will vanish. The camera becomes a way to hold on, even while it puts a screen between you and the moment.
insight.step: At the next good moment, leave the phone in your pocket and describe it to someone later instead.

questions.prompt: Which sounds most like your hobbies?

options.label: One thing I've gone really deep on

insight.reveal: People with one deep hobby often lose track of time in it and get grumpy when interrupted. That same focus usually shows up in love too: you care for few people, but very fully.
insight.step: Teach someone one small thing about your hobby this week and watch how it feels to share it.

options.label: Lots of things tried, none mastered

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you are driven by the first weeks of learning, when progress is fast and visible. People like this often make surprising connections between fields that experts miss.
insight.step: Pick one past hobby and spend twenty minutes on it this week, just to see what you still know.

options.label: I don't really have hobbies anymore

insight.reveal: People who choose this often gave hobbies away slowly, one busy month at a time. The interesting part is what you would pick back up first if you had a free afternoon. That answer is still in you.
insight.step: Spend thirty minutes this weekend on something you used to love, with no goal at all.

options.label: I quit once I'm not quickly good at it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests being bad at something feels more personal to you than it does to most. People who quit early are often very capable, and simply not used to feeling like a beginner.
insight.step: Try something new this week where the only goal is to be bad at it for ten minutes.

questions.prompt: Think about your group chats. Which is true?

options.label: One or two that really matter

insight.reveal: People who keep few active chats often treat messages as conversations, not noise. You probably remember small details people told you weeks ago, and notice when others don't.
insight.step: Reply to one message this week with a question that shows you remembered something.

options.label: Many, and I keep up with all of them

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you are a quiet connector, often the one who knows what everyone is doing. People like this sometimes realise few people check in on them in the same way.
insight.step: Notice who in your chats asks how you are this week, and spend a little more time with them.

options.label: Many, and the unread ones make me guilty

insight.reveal: People who feel guilt over unread chats often hold themselves to a standard of availability no one else asked for. The same rule may make rest feel like something you have to earn.
insight.step: Mute one busy chat for three days and notice whether anyone actually needed you.

options.label: Many, but no one I really talk to

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you are surrounded by contact but missing depth. People who admit this are often closer than they think to one real friendship: it usually starts with one honest message.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: Message one person privately this week, outside the group, and ask how they really are.

questions.prompt: Your ideal birthday dinner looks like…

options.label: A big party. Everyone's invited

insight.reveal: People who want a crowd often feel most like themselves when they can see the whole web of their life in one room. You may enjoy introducing friends to each other more than talking to any one of them.
insight.step: Introduce two people you know who have never met but would get along.

options.label: A few close people around a long table

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you value conversations that can go somewhere. People who choose a small table often judge an evening by whether one real thing got said, not by how loud it was.
insight.step: Invite two people for a simple meal this month, even if it isn't a special day.

options.label: Just one person who really knows me

insight.reveal: People who choose this often find big celebrations of themselves a little uncomfortable. Being truly seen by one person matters more to you than being cheered by many.
insight.step: Tell the person you thought of what they mean to you, before your next birthday comes.

options.label: Alone, with something great to eat

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests attention on your day can feel like pressure more than a gift. People like this often give generously on others' birthdays while quietly hoping their own passes softly.
insight.step: Treat yourself to one great meal alone this week, and let it be enough.

questions.prompt: You win a huge amount of money tomorrow. What do you do first?

options.label: Call my family and share the news

insight.reveal: People whose first move is to share good news often feel joy only once someone else feels it too. The same habit shows up when something good happens at work: it isn't real until you've told someone.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: Share one small piece of good news with someone today, even if it feels too small.

options.label: Stay calm, make a plan, change little

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you trust slow thinking over excitement. People like this often worry that a sudden change would cost them the parts of life that already work, and they're usually right.
insight.step: Write down three things in your life you would keep exactly the same, whatever happened.

options.label: Quit my job that same week

insight.reveal: Your choice says less about money and more about your days. People who answer this way often already know which part of their week they would cut first, and have known for a while.
insight.step: Name the one part of your work week you would drop first, and find one small way to shrink it.

options.label: Tell no one, afraid of how people would change

insight.reveal: People who choose secrecy often have seen money change how people act. Your answer suggests you value being liked for who you are so much that you'd hide good luck to protect it.
insight.step: Notice this week who in your life you'd trust with big news. That list is worth knowing.

questions.prompt: Do brand names on clothes and bags matter to you?

options.label: Not at all. I want comfort

insight.reveal: People who don't care about labels often notice status in other ways: who talks first, who is listened to. You may be less impressed by things and more impressed by how people treat a waiter.
insight.step: This week, notice one sign of status you do care about that has nothing to do with things.

options.label: Quality yes, logos no

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you like luxury you can feel but others can't see. People like this often enjoy being slightly underestimated, and find quiet taste more interesting than loud wealth.
insight.step: Use one 'good' item you're saving this week, on an ordinary day.

options.label: A little. I notice what others wear

insight.reveal: People who choose this are often honest observers: they read rooms quickly and notice small signals others miss. The same skill can turn into quiet comparing on days you feel less sure of yourself.
insight.step: Next time you notice what someone wears, also notice one thing about them that cost nothing.

options.label: Yes. I feel more respected in them

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests clothes work like armour for you, a way to walk into rooms already accepted. People who admit this often had to earn respect early, and still don't fully trust it will be given.
insight.step: Wear your plainest outfit to one ordinary event this week and notice how people actually treat you.

questions.prompt: A close friend suddenly becomes rich. Your honest first feeling?

options.label: Pure happiness for them

insight.reveal: People who feel pure joy here often keep their own scoreboard switched off with friends. The interesting test is a different kind of success: love, talent or looks. Would the joy be just as easy?
insight.step: Congratulate someone this week on a win, and ask them what part of it they're proudest of.

options.label: Curious how they did it

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you turn other people's luck into a puzzle. People like this often learn faster from friends than from books, because they ask the questions others feel too polite to ask.
insight.step: Ask someone you admire this week one specific question about how they got where they are.

options.label: A small sting of envy

insight.reveal: People who admit the sting are usually more honest than most, not less kind. Envy often points at what you want for yourself, and it is strongest with people whose lives look like yours.
insight.step: Next time you feel envy, finish the sentence 'I wish I had…' in your head. That's the real goal.

options.label: Worry they'll leave me behind

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests friendships feel fragile to you when the balance between people shifts. People who feel this often stay loyal for years, and fear that loyalty isn't returned.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety, a worry about rejection, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Reach out to a friend whose life has changed recently, without mentioning the change.

questions.prompt: Which life pulls at you more?

options.label: A small home, lots of free time

insight.reveal: People drawn to a simple life often measure wealth in hours, not things. You may feel richest on a slow morning with nothing booked, and poorest in a busy week, whatever you earn.
insight.step: Give yourself one slow morning this week with nothing scheduled before ten.

options.label: Comfort, plus a few real luxuries

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you know exactly which luxuries are worth it to you and which are noise. People like this tend to spend big on one thing, like a bed, coffee or trips, and almost nothing elsewhere.
insight.step: Name your one 'worth it' luxury and enjoy it slowly this week, without rushing.

options.label: Big success, whatever it takes

insight.reveal: People who choose this often want proof more than possessions: proof they were right, or that they could. Your choice suggests the drive started long before money was the reason.
insight.step: Write down who you'd most want to see your success. Then ask yourself why them.

options.label: I want simple, but I keep chasing more

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests two pulls living in one person. People who feel this often have a clear picture of 'enough' and a fear that stopping early means losing. The gap between them is worth a look.
insight.step: Picture a normal week in your 'enough' life. Find one piece of it you could have this month.

questions.prompt: Dinner with friends who earn more than you. The bill comes. You…

options.label: Split it evenly, no fuss

insight.reveal: People who split without thinking often value the mood of the evening over the exact numbers. You probably remember who was fun more than who ordered the expensive bottle.
insight.step: Next time you eat out, suggest one place that you choose, and see how it feels to lead.

options.label: Quietly do the math in my head

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you carry a quiet calculator into social life. People like this are rarely unfair, but they often feel tension others never notice, and say nothing to keep the peace.
insight.step: Next time it feels uneven, say so lightly once and watch how little drama it causes.

options.label: Order less so I don't overspend

insight.reveal: People who choose this often protect friendships by quietly shrinking themselves. The same habit can show up elsewhere: taking the smaller seat, the worse room, the last turn.
insight.step: At your next meal out, order the thing you actually want, just once.

options.label: Act fine, then stress about it later

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you would rather pay with worry than risk an awkward moment. People like this are often the most generous in the group, and the least likely to let anyone see the cost.
insight.step: Suggest a cheaper plan to one friend this week, like a walk or cooking together.

questions.prompt: You walk into a very fancy hotel lobby. How do you feel?

options.label: At ease. I enjoy places like this

insight.reveal: People who feel at ease in luxury often feel at ease in most rooms. The interesting question is the opposite place: where do you feel out of place? It may say more about you than this answer.
insight.step: Go somewhere this week where you're a beginner, and notice how you carry yourself.

options.label: Excited, like it's a special treat

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you still feel wonder at nice things, which many people lose. People like this often get more joy from one rare treat than others get from daily luxury.
insight.step: Plan one small special treat for later this week, and enjoy the waiting as much as the treat.

options.label: A bit bored. It's all for show

insight.reveal: People who see through luxury often have a sharp eye for what is performed. The same eye may make it hard for you to enjoy compliments or nice gestures without checking if they're real.
insight.step: Accept the next compliment you get with just 'thank you', no checking, no deflecting.

options.label: Like someone will notice I don't belong

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests a quiet voice that checks whether you are allowed to be somewhere. People who hear it often feel it in meetings and new groups too, even when they are welcome.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves.
insight.step: Ask a friend which room they think you belong in most. Their answer may surprise you.

questions.prompt: You meet someone wearing a very expensive watch. First thought?

options.label: Nice watch. That's it

insight.reveal: People who stop at 'nice watch' often give others a clean first impression. You may judge people by what they do next, and be slower than most to decide who someone is.
insight.step: Next time you meet someone new, guess one thing about them, then check it later.

options.label: I wonder what they do for work

insight.reveal: This answer suggests your mind turns objects into stories about paths and choices. People like this often compare careers more than possessions, quietly mapping other lives against their own.
insight.step: Ask one person this week how they ended up in their job, and listen for the turning point.

options.label: They're trying to impress someone

insight.reveal: People who read status as performance often value humility a lot, sometimes so much that they hide their own wins. The question is whether you let yourself enjoy nice things without suspicion.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Mention one thing you're proud of to someone this week, plainly, without a joke.

options.label: I quietly compare myself and come up short

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests other people's things can feel like a score you're being measured against. People who notice this often compare on many fronts, and rarely count the things they have that others want.
insight.step: Write down three things someone might envy about your life, then read them once a day this week.

questions.prompt: Growing up, how did money feel in your home?

options.label: Rarely talked about. It was just there

insight.reveal: People who grew up with money in the background often find money talk awkward as adults. You may know less about your friends' money lives than about their love lives.
insight.step: Ask someone you trust one simple money question this week, like what they enjoy spending on.

options.label: Tight, but we managed

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who still check prices out of habit, even when they don't need to. The same habit can make generous spending on yourself feel strangely like breaking a rule.
insight.step: Buy yourself one small thing this week without checking the price first.

options.label: Money caused arguments

insight.reveal: People who heard money fights growing up often feel tension in their body when money comes up, even in happy moments. You may avoid money talk with a partner to keep the peace you didn't have then.
insight.step: Start one calm, short money chat this week with someone close, at a relaxed moment.

options.label: Something I still feel uneasy about today

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests the money feelings of childhood still live in your adult days. People who notice this often find their unease doesn't track their bank balance, which shows it's about safety, not numbers.
insight.step: Next time money worry rises, ask: 'Is this about today, or about back then?' and just notice the answer.

questions.prompt: You get some unexpected extra money this month. Where does it go?

options.label: Put aside for later

insight.reveal: People who put surprise money aside often feel safer than they feel happy. The twist: they also tend to delay small joys long after they could easily afford them.
insight.step: Do one small thing this week you've been 'saving up' to enjoy, even a tiny one.

options.label: A meal or trip with people I love

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you turn money into memories with people in them. Those choices tend to grow in value over time, because the story gets retold every time you meet.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: Suggest a simple shared plan with someone this week, like a picnic or a cheap dinner.

options.label: Something just for me

insight.reveal: People who choose this often spend most of the year putting others first. A gift to yourself may be one of the few times you act as if your own wants count as much as everyone else's.
insight.step: Notice one want of your own this week and say it out loud to someone.

options.label: It's gone before I even notice

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests money slips into the flow of small daily wants. People like this often love living in the moment, and find that later can feel very far away from now.
insight.research: People with stronger present bias, preferring smaller rewards now over bigger ones later, are more likely to carry credit card debt.
insight.step: For three days, write down one small thing you spent on each evening, just to see the pattern.

questions.prompt: Your income doubles overnight. Would you be happier?

options.label: Yes, clearly

insight.reveal: People who answer a clear yes often know exactly which daily stress money would remove. That clarity is useful: it shows which of your problems are about money and which ones aren't.
insight.research: For most people, happiness keeps rising with income; for the least happy group, it stops rising above a fairly high income.
insight.step: Name the one daily stress more money would fix, and find one free way to soften it this week.

options.label: A bit, then I'd get used to it

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you already know how fast new comforts become normal. People like this are often hard to impress with things, and easier to delight with surprises.
insight.step: Surprise someone with a small unexpected gesture this week and notice your own mood after.

options.label: No. My real problems aren't about money

insight.reveal: People who choose this often carry one problem that no amount of money touches: a relationship, a choice, a feeling. Your answer suggests you already know which one it is.
insight.research: For most people, happiness keeps rising with income; for the least happy group, it stops rising above a fairly high income.
insight.step: Spend ten quiet minutes this week on the problem money can't fix, just thinking it through.

options.label: I'd mostly worry about losing it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests that for you, having more means having more to lose. People like this often feel safest in the middle of things, neither on top nor at the bottom, where nothing can fall far.
insight.step: Next time you get something good, say 'this is good right now' before your mind jumps to losing it.

questions.prompt: If money and fear disappeared tomorrow, what would you do first?

options.label: Travel far, for a long time
