insight.reveal: People who choose travel often want distance as much as adventure: a space where no one expects them to be who they usually are. The interesting part is who you would become there.
insight.step: Spend one afternoon this week somewhere in your area where no one knows you.

options.label: Start the thing I keep talking about

insight.reveal: This answer suggests your dream is already specific, which puts you ahead of most. People with a named dream often wait for a perfect start date that keeps moving a little further away.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Write one when-then plan: 'When it's Saturday 10 a.m., I will spend 20 minutes on my idea.'

options.label: Honestly, I don't know what I'd want

insight.reveal: People who answer this way have often spent years being good at what's needed rather than what's wanted. Not knowing isn't empty: it often means your wants have been too quiet to hear.
insight.step: Each evening this week, note one moment that made you feel more alive than usual.

options.label: Leave a job or relationship I've outgrown

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you already know what you would change, and that fear, not clarity, is what's missing. People who admit this often find that saying it, even silently, is the first real step.
insight.step: Write down one small thing you could change about that situation this month, without leaving it.

questions.prompt: Which kind of regret visits you most often?

options.label: Something I said

insight.reveal: People who replay their words often care deeply how they land on others. The same people are usually the first to apologise, and the last to accept an apology for themselves.
insight.step: Next time a sentence replays in your head, ask the person directly if it bothered them.

options.label: A chance I didn't take

insight.reveal: This answer suggests the roads you didn't take still feel open in your mind. People like this often regret inaction more than mistakes, which makes them braver than they think when the next chance comes.
insight.step: Say yes to one small invitation this week that you'd normally talk yourself out of.

options.label: Someone I lost touch with

insight.reveal: People who carry this regret often assume the other person moved on. In many cases they are thinking of you too, and waiting for the same first message you're afraid to send.
insight.step: Send that person one short message this week. No need to explain the gap.

options.label: Years spent being who others wanted

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you now see the gap between who you were and who you showed. People who notice this have usually already started closing it. The regret itself is a sign of change.
insight.step: Make one small choice this week purely because you want it, not because it pleases anyone.

questions.prompt: Two offers: a safe job, or a risky one doing what you love. You…

options.label: Take the safe job

insight.reveal: People who choose safety often feed their passions on the side, where no one can take them away. You may protect what you love by keeping it out of the hands of a boss.
insight.step: Give one hour this week to the thing you love, with no plan to turn it into money.

options.label: Ask for time and make long lists

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you trust lists more than your gut, though often your gut has already chosen. People like this sometimes make lists to talk themselves out of what they already want.
insight.step: Next big choice, flip a coin. Notice which side you hoped for while it was in the air.

options.label: Take the risk, sort it out later

insight.reveal: People who leap often believe they can handle almost any fall, and usually they're right. The twist: they sometimes leap to escape boredom, not to reach a dream.
insight.step: Before your next leap, write one line on what you're running to, not just from.

options.label: Take the safe one and wonder forever

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you know your heart and your fear well, and fear often wins the vote. People like this often take bigger risks for others than for themselves.
insight.step: Take one tiny risk for yourself this week, something you'd easily encourage a friend to do.

questions.prompt: Who knows about your biggest dream?

options.label: Everyone. I talk about it a lot

insight.reveal: People who share dreams widely often use other people as a promise they can't break. For some it works; for others, the talking feels so good it quietly replaces the doing.
insight.step: This week, take one step toward your dream before telling anyone about it.

options.label: One or two close people

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you guard your dream like something fragile. People like this often choose their audience carefully, picking the ones who will believe in it without asking for proof.
insight.step: Update one of those people on your dream this week, even if there's little progress.

options.label: No one. Saying it would make it real

insight.reveal: People who keep their dream secret often fear the look on someone's face more than failure itself. A dream that is never spoken can't be judged, but it also can't be helped.
insight.step: Tell one kind person a small part of your dream this week, just one sentence.

options.label: I've stopped admitting it even to myself

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests the dream got quiet to protect you from wanting it. People who say this often still feel it in odd moments: a song, a film, someone else's success that stings more than it should.
insight.step: Notice the next time someone else's success stings. Ask what it reminds you of.

questions.prompt: Someone your age achieves exactly your dream. You feel…

options.label: Inspired. It's possible!

insight.reveal: People who feel inspired by peers often see the world as having room for everyone. The same belief makes you a good friend to ambitious people, who often feel judged elsewhere.
insight.step: Look up how that person started, and find one step they took that you could take too.

options.label: Fired up to catch up

insight.reveal: This answer suggests a rival is better fuel for you than a goal. People like this often do their best work when someone is just ahead, and drift when they're alone in front.
insight.step: Choose a friendly 'rival' this week and share one small goal with them.

options.label: Quietly crushed for a day or two

insight.reveal: People who feel crushed often have a timeline in their head for where they should be by now. The pain is less about the other person and more about that private clock.
insight.step: Write down where you thought you'd be by now. Then cross out the date and keep the goal.

options.label: Relief. Now I don't have to try

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests the dream carried a weight of pressure along with the hope. People who feel relief here often discover the dream was partly someone else's, and their own is still waiting.
insight.step: Ask yourself this week: which of my goals did I choose, and which did I inherit?

questions.prompt: It's Sunday night. What's mostly on your mind?

options.label: Plans for the week ahead

insight.reveal: People who plan on Sunday nights often feel calm only when the week has a shape. The same need can make surprise weekends feel more stressful than fun.
insight.step: Leave one evening this week totally unplanned and see what you choose to do with it.

options.label: Not much. I'm relaxed

insight.reveal: People who stay calm on Sunday nights usually have work that fits their life, or a strong wall between the two. Either way, you have something many people spend years trying to build.
insight.step: Notice what keeps your Sunday calm, and protect that one habit this week.

options.label: A quiet 'is this it?'

insight.reveal: People who feel the 'is this it?' moment are usually not unhappy, but unfinished. The question often comes back at the same time each week, a clue that it's about routine more than your whole life.
insight.step: Add one new thing to next Sunday evening, even a small one, and see if the feeling changes.

options.label: The life I'd live if I were braver

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you can see a clear second life next to your current one. People who carry this picture often already know its first step, and keep it waiting for the right Monday.
insight.step: This Monday, do one five-minute action from that braver life.

questions.prompt: When you set a big goal, what usually happens?

options.label: I make a plan and stick to it

insight.reveal: People who follow through on plans often find goals easy and rest hard. The same discipline can make it tricky to drop a goal that no longer fits, just because you started it.
insight.research: Personality traits predict life outcomes such as health, divorce and career success about as well as family income and intelligence do.
insight.step: Look at one current goal this week and ask: do I still want this, or just want to finish it?

options.label: Start strong, fade by week three

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you run on excitement, and excitement runs out before the habit forms. People like this often succeed best when the goal is tiny and the start is easy.
insight.research: In one study, new daily habits took a median of 66 days to become automatic, and missing a single day did not ruin progress.
insight.step: Pick a goal you dropped and restart it at a size so small it feels silly.

options.label: I keep it vague so I can't fail

insight.reveal: People who keep goals vague often care a lot about getting them right. Vague is safe: no one, including you, can say you missed. It also means no one can say you made it.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Turn one vague goal into a when-then plan: 'When X happens, I will do Y.'

options.label: I avoid setting goals. They stress me

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests goals feel like a test you might fail. People like this often grow more through curiosity than through targets: they follow what interests them and end up far.
insight.step: Instead of a goal, pick one question you're curious about and explore it for 20 minutes.

questions.prompt: Whose life do you secretly envy a little?

options.label: Someone who travels with no fixed home

insight.reveal: People who envy the traveller often want lightness more than travel: fewer things to look after, fewer people expecting them. The wish may be pointing at what feels heavy right now.
insight.step: Remove one small duty from your week that no one would really miss.

options.label: Someone who makes things for a living

insight.reveal: This answer suggests a part of you wants proof of your days, something you can hold. People like this often feel restless in jobs where the work disappears into emails and meetings.
insight.step: Make one small thing with your hands this week: a meal, a drawing, a repair.

options.label: An old friend who chose differently

insight.reveal: People who envy an old friend are often looking at a road they once stood at too. The envy is less about that person and more about a version of you who might have gone with them.
insight.step: Get in touch with that friend this month and ask what they miss about the road you took.

options.label: A version of me who made another choice

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you keep a clear picture of an alternate life. People who do this often edit out that version's problems. The most useful question is which piece of it you could still have.
insight.step: Name one quality of that 'other you' and try acting with it for one day this week.

questions.prompt: At 90, looking back, what would hurt most?

options.label: Places I never saw

insight.reveal: People who fear missing places often feel most alive when everything around them is new. Your choice suggests routine might drain you faster than it drains others.
insight.step: Take a different route to somewhere you go every day, at least once this week.

options.label: Work I never finished or made

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you want to leave something behind with your name on it. People like this often feel time pressure others don't, and judge good days by what got built.
insight.step: Spend 25 minutes this week on the thing you'd most hate to leave unmade.

options.label: Love I didn't say out loud

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel love deeply but show it sideways, through help, jokes or presence. The words feel too big, so they wait for a moment that never feels right.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: Tell one person this week, in plain words, one thing you love about them.

options.label: Knowing I played it safe on purpose

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you already feel the cost of caution while you're paying it. People who see this clearly at any age are often closer to changing than people who never ask.
insight.step: Do one thing this week that your 90-year-old self would be glad you did.

questions.prompt: When you really want something from someone, what do you do?

options.label: Ask for it directly

insight.reveal: People who ask directly often believe a 'no' is just information, not a judgement. The same ease can surprise others, who may need a little more warm-up than you do.
insight.step: Next time you ask for something, add one sentence about why it matters to you.

options.label: Drop hints and hope

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you want people to notice your wishes without you naming them, as proof they care. People rarely read hints as well as hinters hope, so the test is often failed unfairly.
insight.step: Turn one hint into a plain request this week: 'I'd love it if…'

options.label: Wait until someone offers

insight.reveal: People who wait for offers often hate the idea of taking more than their share. The cost is quiet: good things go to people who simply asked first.
insight.step: Ask for one small thing this week that you would normally wait to be offered.

options.label: Tell myself I didn't want it anyway

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests that not wanting is safer than wanting and not getting. People who do this often seem easygoing to others, while a list of quiet 'never minds' grows inside.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment avoidance, a discomfort with closeness, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Catch one 'never mind' this week and say the real wish out loud instead.

questions.prompt: How do you most often show a partner affection?

options.label: Small touches during the day

insight.reveal: People who show love through small touches often notice when touch is missing before they notice anything else. A day without a hand on the shoulder may feel colder to you than a missed call.
insight.step: Next time your partner walks past, give them a light touch for no reason at all.

options.label: Saying it out loud, often

insight.reveal: This answer suggests words feel like a promise to you, not decoration. People who say it often sometimes worry when a partner says it less, even when every other sign is there.
insight.step: This week, notice one way your partner shows love without words, and tell them you saw it.

options.label: I show it, but rarely say it

insight.reveal: People who show rather than say often grew up where love was a fixed roof, not a sentence. You may be giving more than your partner realises, simply in a language they don't always read.
insight.step: Pair one thing you do for your partner this week with one sentence about why.

options.label: I wait for them to show it first

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests reaching out first feels like a risk of not being met. People like this often feel a lot of affection that stays behind a door, waiting for proof it is safe.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance, and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Make the first warm move once this week, small and simple, and notice what comes back.

questions.prompt: What does a truly romantic evening look like to you?

options.label: Dinner somewhere new

insight.reveal: People who find newness romantic often feel attraction rise when they see their partner in an unfamiliar setting. A new place makes a familiar person a little mysterious again.
insight.step: Suggest one place neither of you has been for your next evening together.

options.label: Cooking together at home

insight.reveal: This answer suggests romance for you lives inside teamwork. People like this often feel most drawn to a partner while doing something side by side, not sitting face to face.
insight.step: Cook one meal together this week with phones in another room.

options.label: A long talk with phones away

insight.reveal: People who choose talk as romance often feel desire follow closeness, not the other way round. Being really listened to may feel more intimate to you than any candlelit setting.
insight.step: Ask your partner one question tonight you've never asked them before.

options.label: Honestly, we've stopped planning these

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests romance slipped quietly behind daily life. People who notice this are often the ones who miss it most, and missing it is a good sign: the wish is still alive.
insight.step: Plan one small evening for this week, even just a walk, and call it a date out loud.

questions.prompt: What usually draws you to someone first?

options.label: They make me laugh

insight.reveal: People drawn to humour often read it as a sign of quick thinking and safety. The same people can lose interest fast when a partner stops being playful, even if everything else is fine.
insight.step: Start something playful with your partner or a friend this week, just to see who joins in.

options.label: Their confidence

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you're drawn to people who seem settled in themselves. Often it means you want someone steady enough that you can relax, and stop holding things together.
insight.step: Notice one moment this week when you felt fully at ease with someone. What made it so?

options.label: The way they look at me

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel attraction grow from being wanted. Desire for you may start as a mirror, and it can fade quickly if that look of interest goes away.
insight.step: Look at your partner for a few seconds longer than usual this week, and see what changes.

options.label: Someone a little hard to read

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests uncertainty feels exciting, maybe more than comfort does. People like this often mistake the rush of not knowing for chemistry, and find calm partners hard to fall for at first.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety, a worry about rejection, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time someone feels 'too easy', give it one more conversation before deciding.

questions.prompt: When one of you leaves the house, what happens?

options.label: Always a kiss or hug goodbye

insight.reveal: People who keep a goodbye ritual often protect the relationship with small daily habits more than big gestures. You probably notice right away when a goodbye is skipped.
insight.step: Make tomorrow's goodbye last five seconds longer than usual.

options.label: Sometimes, if we remember

insight.reveal: This answer suggests affection is there but runs on autopilot. People like this often feel close in big moments and drift a little in the ordinary days between them.
insight.step: Pick one daily moment, leaving or arriving, and make it a small ritual this week.

options.label: Rarely. We're deep in routine

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel comfortable more than close. Routine is a sign of trust, but small touches are often the first thing to go, and the easiest to bring back.
insight.step: Surprise your partner with a goodbye hug tomorrow, with no explanation.

options.label: I'd like to, but feel shy starting it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests that even with someone close, reaching out can feel exposed. People who feel this often assume their partner doesn't want it, when the partner is waiting too.
insight.step: Start one goodbye touch this week. Keep it small, and let it be enough.

questions.prompt: When do you feel the strongest desire for a partner?

options.label: After we've laughed together

insight.reveal: People whose desire follows laughter often need to feel safe and light before they feel wanting. A stressful week may quietly dim your desire more than you realise.
insight.step: Share something funny with your partner this week, on purpose, and notice the mood after.

options.label: Seeing them confident in their element

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you feel desire when you see your partner as a separate person, not just part of 'us'. A bit of distance and admiration may do more for you than closeness alone.
insight.step: Watch your partner do something they're good at this week, and tell them what you noticed.

options.label: After some time apart

insight.reveal: People who feel desire after time apart often need space to miss someone before they can want them. Constant closeness may feel loving to you, but not always exciting.
insight.step: Spend an evening apart this week doing your own thing, then notice how you feel on return.

options.label: Oddly, after we've had tension

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests closeness feels most urgent when it was briefly at risk. People like this often feel relief and desire arrive together, which can make making up feel stronger than calm days.
insight.step: This week, try creating that same closeness on a calm day, with an unexpected warm moment.

questions.prompt: In your relationship, who usually starts things in the bedroom?

options.label: Pretty equal, it goes both ways

insight.reveal: People in a balanced pattern often feel wanted without having to keep checking. The quiet risk is assuming the balance will stay without anyone ever talking about it.
insight.step: Tell your partner one thing you like about how they show they want you.

options.label: Mostly me

insight.reveal: People who usually initiate often carry a hidden question: would anything happen if I stopped? Your choice suggests confidence on the surface, and maybe a wish to be the one pursued sometimes.
insight.step: Tell your partner, kindly and outside the bedroom, that you'd love them to start things sometimes.

options.label: Mostly my partner

insight.reveal: This answer often belongs to people who feel desire as a response, not a spark. That is common and normal, but your partner may read your waiting as less wanting than you feel.
insight.step: Make one small first move this week, even just a lingering kiss, and see how it lands.

options.label: Neither of us, lately

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests a quiet standoff where each person waits for the other. People in this place often both miss it, and each believes the other has stopped wanting it.
insight.research: In large samples, couples' well-being rose with how often they had sex up to about once a week, then levelled off.
insight.step: Start a gentle chat this week: 'I miss us being close. Do you?' Nothing more is needed.

questions.prompt: How do you honestly feel about how often you and a partner are intimate?

options.label: It feels about right

insight.reveal: People who feel the rhythm is right often judge intimacy by how close they feel, not by counting. Your answer suggests you trust the relationship enough not to keep score.
insight.research: In large samples, couples' well-being rose with how often they had sex up to about once a week, then levelled off.
insight.step: Tell your partner one recent moment of closeness you enjoyed, in or out of bed.

options.label: I'd like more

insight.reveal: This answer often hides a deeper wish: to feel chosen. People who want more often feel desire as reassurance, so a quiet week can feel like a message even when it isn't one.
insight.step: Ask your partner what helps them feel in the mood, and just listen to the answer.

options.label: I'd honestly like less

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel guilty about it, though it's a common and honest place to be. Desire usually responds to stress, sleep and feeling heard more than to the partner themselves.
insight.step: Notice this week which kinds of closeness you do want, and share one with your partner.

options.label: We never talk about it, so I'm not sure

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests intimacy is happening, or not, in silence. Couples who never discuss it often each guess what the other wants, and both guess wrong in the same careful direction.
insight.step: Pick a relaxed moment this week and ask, lightly: 'Are you happy with how close we are?'

questions.prompt: Could you tell a partner plainly what you enjoy in bed?

options.label: Easily. We talk openly

insight.reveal: People who talk openly about intimacy usually find it easier to talk about other hard things too: money, family, fears. Your openness here may be the root of a lot of your relationship's strength.
insight.step: Ask your partner one open question this week about what they've been enjoying lately.

options.label: Only if they ask first

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you're open, but you need an invitation. People like this often assume a partner would ask if they wanted to know, while the partner assumes you'd say.
insight.step: Give the invitation yourself: ask your partner what they enjoy, and let them ask you back.

options.label: I hint or show instead of saying

insight.reveal: People who hint often find words in this area feel more exposing than the act itself. That's a striking twist: closeness is easy for you, but naming it can feel like too much.
insight.step: Say one short, positive sentence this week about something you enjoyed together.

options.label: I've never really said it

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests your own pleasure has stayed private, even from people you trust. People who admit this often put a partner's comfort first and their own wants somewhere quiet.
insight.step: Think of one thing you enjoy, and find a kind, simple way to tell your partner this week.

questions.prompt: A partner suggests trying something new together in bed. You feel…

options.label: Curious. Let's talk about it

insight.reveal: People whose first reaction is curiosity often see intimacy as something a couple builds together, not a fixed routine. The talk itself may be part of the excitement for you.
insight.step: Ask your partner one 'what if we…' question this week, about anything, and see where it goes.

options.label: Excited. I've wanted that too

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you've been carrying wishes you hadn't voiced. People like this often wait for a partner to open the door, then are surprised how easy walking through it was.
insight.step: Open the next door yourself: share one small new idea with your partner this week.

options.label: Nervous, but willing to talk

insight.reveal: People who feel nervous but open often care a lot about getting it right. Your choice suggests trust matters more to you than novelty, and with trust, new things feel safe to try.
insight.step: Tell your partner what would help you feel at ease with something new. Only yes means yes.

options.label: Worried I'm not enough as I am

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests a new idea can sound like a review of you. People who feel this often hear 'let's add' as 'you're missing', when most partners mean it as an invitation, not a complaint.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety, a worry about rejection, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Ask your partner directly: 'What do you love about us as we are?' and let the answer land.

questions.prompt: When do you feel most desirable?

options.label: After a day where I did well

insight.reveal: People who feel desirable after success often link being wanted with being capable. Your attraction may rise and fall with your work week more than with your mirror.
insight.step: On your next good day, tell your partner about it, and notice whether closeness follows.

options.label: When I've made an effort to dress up

insight.reveal: This answer suggests confidence for you is something you can put on, like a key that unlocks a bolder self. People like this often enjoy being seen more than they'd ever say out loud.
insight.step: Dress up a little this week for no special reason, and see if your mood follows.

options.label: When my partner can't stop looking

insight.reveal: People who choose this often feel desirable through another person's eyes more than their own. It's warm when the looks come, and can feel cold on days they don't.
insight.step: Find one moment this week when you feel attractive alone, with no one watching.

options.label: Rarely. I wait to be told

insight.reveal: Your choice suggests you see yourself through a harsher filter than others do. People who feel this are often found far more attractive than they believe, and rarely believe it when told.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves.
insight.step: Next compliment you get on how you look, just say 'thank you' and don't argue with it.
